chapters.title: Cell
chapters.subtitle: The ventricular action potential
chapters.lede: A ventricular cell rests at a steady negative voltage, fires when a neighbour excites it, and takes hundreds of milliseconds to recover. Different ion currents shape each phase of this action potential, and the QRS complex, ST segment and T wave of the electrocardiogram (ECG) fall in different phases.
chapters.body:
The action potential

Between beats a ventricular myocyte holds its interior about 85 mV negative to the outside. When current from an activated neighbour depolarizes it past threshold, it fires an action potential (AP): a rapid rise, a plateau, and a return to rest. Its phases are numbered 0 to 4, and each is set by a different balance between inward currents, which carry positive charge into the cell, and outward currents, which carry it out. Its length, the action potential duration (APD), is measured from the upstroke to 50% or 90% repolarization (APD50, APD90), and the steepness of the upstroke as its maximum rate of rise (max dV/dt).

Phase by phase

Phase 0, the upstroke, is a large inward sodium current (INa) through voltage-gated sodium channels, which open in under a millisecond. In phase 1, the notch, the sodium channels inactivate and the transient outward potassium current (Ito) partly repolarizes the membrane. Phase 2, the plateau, is a balance between the inward L-type calcium current (ICa,L) and the outward delayed rectifier potassium currents, rapid (IKr) and slow (IKs); the cell stays depolarized and refractory for hundreds of milliseconds. In phase 3 the calcium channels inactivate, the outward potassium currents prevail, and the inward rectifier current (IK1) helps complete repolarization. In phase 4, IK1 holds the resting potential.

The model on this page

The cell in the figure is the minimal ventricular model of Bueno-Orovio, Cherry and Fenton, built to reproduce the action potential shapes, upstroke velocities and rate dependence of human epicardial, endocardial and midmyocardial cells. It has one voltage and three gating variables, and it groups every membrane current into three: a fast inward current, a slow inward current and a slow outward current, standing for the summed sodium, calcium and potassium currents. These are phenomenological groupings; the model does not describe individual channels. The equations and parameter sets come from an open-source implementation of the model, and the epicardial set matches the one its authors reprinted. The cell is paced with a brief stimulus until its action potential stops changing from beat to beat, and the last beat is shown. One control scales the fast inward current, as a sodium-channel blocker would. The maximum rate of rise falls with it, while the duration barely changes. Another scales the whole slow outward current. Turning it down lengthens the action potential, as potassium-channel blockers do, but the model cannot single out one channel such as IKr.

Three kinds of ventricular cell

Cells differ across the ventricular wall: epicardial cells show a prominent spike and dome, endocardial cells a smaller notch, and, in dog hearts, midmyocardial (M) cells the longest action potential, about 100 ms longer than the other two. In the model only the epicardial cell has a notch, and the M cell outlasts the others by more than 100 ms. In wedges of non-failing human left ventricle paced every 2000 ms, the action potential duration to 80% repolarization was 383 ± 21 ms in the subepicardium, 455 ± 20 ms in the midmyocardium and 494 ± 22 ms in the subendocardium, with islands of longer midmyocardial action potentials in three of five hearts. In whole donor hearts, repolarization showed no late midmural region. The model's M cell is better read as a cell type than as a layer of the intact wall.

Rate

At faster rates the action potential shortens. In the model, the gate of the slow inward current recovers between beats; a shorter diastolic interval leaves it less recovered, the plateau's inward current is smaller, and repolarization comes sooner. The model was built to reproduce this restitution of action potential duration in human cells. The same shortening across the ventricles is why the QT interval shortens as the heart rate rises and is reported corrected for rate.

From one cell to the ECG

The ECG reflects differences in transmembrane voltage between cells. During the QRS the ventricles' cells pass through phase 0 one after another, as activation crosses them. During the ST segment every cell is in its plateau at about the same voltage, so little current flows between them. The T wave arises during phase 3, because cells repolarize at different times. The T wave common to all leads (van Oosterom's dominant T wave) is shaped like the rate at which the mean action potential of the cells at the heart's surfaces falls during recovery, and peaks at their mean repolarization time; how tall it is in a given lead depends on how widely the recovery times are spread (chapter 02). In the lower panel this cell's upstroke is placed at the mean activation time of its layer of the simulated left ventricle, and its phase 3 is shaded. The cells of the simulated heart all follow the same simpler action potential template, timed by fitting the whole heart's ECG to real recordings. They do not use this model, and the two action potentials differ by tens of milliseconds.
keypoints: Phase 0 is the sodium current’s upstroke, phase 1 the transient outward notch, phase 2 the plateau of inward calcium against outward potassium current, phase 3 repolarization by potassium currents, and phase 4 rest, held by I<sub>K1</sub>.
The QRS occurs while the ventricles’ cells pass through phase 0, the ST segment during their plateau, and the T wave during phase 3.
Less fast inward current slows the upstroke with little change in duration; less outward current lengthens the action potential.
Faster rates shorten the action potential, which is why the QT interval is corrected for rate.
The model on this page groups all membrane currents into three phenomenological currents; it does not describe individual channels.

chapters.title: Dipole
chapters.subtitle: From a wavefront to the heart vector
chapters.lede: Wherever active cells meet resting ones, current flows, and the boundary acts as a sheet of tiny dipoles. Added together they make one arrow, the heart vector, and each of the twelve leads records that arrow from its own direction.
chapters.body:
A wavefront is a layer of dipoles

Where an active cell meets a resting neighbour, their interiors differ by most of an action potential. Current flows through the junctions between them from the active cell into the resting one, and returns through the fluid outside. Seen from outside, each such boundary is a current source beside a sink, which together make a dipole. Its arrow points from the active cell toward the resting one, the way the wave is travelling. An electrode on the side the arrows point to records a positive potential; one behind them, a negative potential. A unipolar electrode therefore records an upward deflection as a wave comes toward it and a downward deflection as the wave moves away, and both, one after the other, as a wave passes beneath it.

Adding the arrows

The strip in the figure is a toy, flat and two-dimensional, but it follows the same rule as the heart for adding the fields of its dipoles. Every boundary between two cells that differ in voltage has an arrow. The electrode's signal is the sum of all the arrows' fields, and the arrow beside the strip is their vector sum. A straight front crossing the strip adds up to one arrow along its path. A wave started at a point inside the strip spreads as a ring whose arrows point outward in every direction: they sum to zero, and an electrode anywhere outside the ring records nothing, however close it is. The signal appears only when the ring reaches the edges of the tissue and is no longer a closed curve. Once every cell is active there is no boundary left, and the signal returns to zero although the whole strip is depolarized.

The equivalent double layer

Outside the tissue, the arrows on the wavefront give exactly the same field as a double layer spread over the tissue's boundary, whose strength at each point follows the transmembrane voltage of the cells there. In heart muscle, whose conductivity differs along and across the fibres, this equivalence holds when the ratio of the two is the same inside and outside the cells. van Oosterom built a model of the electrocardiogram on this idea: the heart's whole electrical activity expressed as an equivalent double layer on the boundary of the ventricles, driven by the timing of depolarization and repolarization of the cells next to it. In this model, only boundaries between active and resting tissue make current, so tissue that is all at rest, or all active, produces a flat line; a wave buried inside the wall produces no signal until it reaches the endocardium or the epicardium. In the same model, the amplitude of the T wave is proportional to the dispersion of repolarization times over the ventricular surface. With the strip's sources drawn on the tissue's edge, the arrows are different, but their sum and the signal at any electrode off the tissue are unchanged.

The heart vector

In the heart the fronts are surfaces in three dimensions, and at each instant all their dipoles add up to one vector, the heart vector. The simulation computes it with the equivalent double layer, from the transmembrane voltage on every surface of the simulated heart. During the QRS the heart vector swings from the small early force of the septum, which activates first, to the large leftward force of the left ventricle, and ends pointing toward the last regions to activate, at the base. Its tip traces a loop, the QRS loop of the vectorcardiogram.

Projection on each lead

Each lead records the heart vector from its own direction. Its voltage is the projection of the heart vector on the lead vector: the arrow's shadow on the lead's axis, scaled by the lead's sensitivity (the lead vector's length). The simulation takes the lead vectors from Dower's transformation, in the Frank frame, in which X points to the patient's left, Y to the feet and Z to the back. The direction shown for the heart vector is measured in Frank's X–Y plane; the limb leads, whose lead vectors chapter 03 explains, report a frontal angle that can differ from it by tens of degrees. For the six limb leads the shadow in the figure, times the lead's sensitivity, is exactly the voltage on the tracing. The chest electrodes sit close to the heart, where a single central dipole describes the field less well, so the simulation adds a near-field correction to V1 to V6; the grey traces show the projection of the heart vector alone.
keypoints: The boundary between active and resting tissue is a layer of dipoles pointing the way the wave travels.
An electrode records an upward deflection as the wave approaches, a downward one as it leaves, and both, one after the other, as it passes beneath.
A closed front produces no signal outside it, and neither does tissue that is all at rest or all active.

In the equivalent-double-layer model, which assumes the ratio of conductivity along and across the fibres is the same inside and outside the cells, the wavefront’s field outside the heart equals that of a double layer on the heart’s surfaces, whose strength follows the local transmembrane voltage; a wave inside the wall is silent until it reaches a surface.
At each instant the dipoles sum to one heart vector, and each lead records its projection on that lead’s direction, scaled by the lead’s sensitivity.

chapters.title: Leads
chapters.subtitle: Twelve views of one vector
chapters.lede: At each instant the electrical activity of the heart adds up to one vector. Each of the twelve leads records the vector’s projection, or shadow, on its own axis.
chapters.body:
The heart vector and its projections

Einthoven treated the heart as a dipole, a single source whose strength and direction change through the beat. The dipole is represented by a vector, the heart vector. In his model the voltage in a lead is the projection of the heart vector onto the line that defines the lead. When the vector points toward a lead’s positive pole the pen moves up, when it points away the pen moves down, and when it lies across the lead the trace stays near the baseline. A lead that is perpendicular to the vector at the start or end of a wave records that part as flat, so a duration measured in one lead tends to be shorter than the same duration measured across all twelve.

The limb leads and Einthoven’s law

Four electrodes go on the arms and legs, distal to the shoulders and hips; the right leg (RL) electrode is an electronic reference that helps reject noise. Lead I is the left arm minus the right arm (LA − RA), lead II the left leg minus the right arm (LL − RA), and lead III the left leg minus the left arm (LL − LA). Because the three form a closed loop, Kirchhoff’s law gives Einthoven’s law: II = I + III at every instant. The law does not depend on where the electrodes sit, but drawing them at the corners of an equilateral triangle, Einthoven’s triangle, puts the three leads in one frame.

Wilson’s central terminal and Goldberger’s leads

Wilson averaged the three limb electrodes into a central terminal, (RA + LA + LL)/3, to serve as a reference potential. Goldberger left the exploring electrode out of that average, which makes his augmented leads 50% larger than the same electrodes measured against Wilson’s terminal: aVR = RA − (LA + LL)/2, aVL = LA − (RA + LL)/2 and aVF = LL − (RA + LA)/2. Each reduces to a combination of I and II, so the six frontal leads carry only two independent signals, and an electrocardiograph measures two and computes the other four. Moved to one centre, the three sides of Einthoven’s triangle and Goldberger’s three leads divide the circle every 30°, with lead I at 0° and aVF at +90°. This is the hexaxial reference system, the frame in which the frontal QRS axis, the direction of the mean QRS vector, is expressed; in adults that axis normally lies between −30° and +90°.

The chest leads

V1 sits in the fourth intercostal space (ICS) at the right sternal border and V2 in the fourth ICS at the left sternal border; V4 sits in the fifth ICS in the midclavicular line (MCL), and V3 midway between V2 and V4; V5 lies in the horizontal plane of V4 at the anterior axillary line (AAL), or midway between V4 and V6 if that line is unclear, and V6 in the same plane at the midaxillary line. For the time being, the electrodes go under the breast in women. Each chest electrode is paired with Wilson’s terminal, and from V1 to V6 they progress leftward and slightly inferiorly across the chest, so together they view the heart in roughly the horizontal plane. No chest lead can be computed from the others, so a 12-lead electrocardiogram (ECG) holds eight independent signals, two from the limbs and six from the chest. The potential at an exploring electrode comes from every source active in the heart at that instant, including muscle far from the electrode.

Lead vectors

The torso is not a uniform conductor. Burger and colleagues treated each lead as a vector whose direction differs from the line between its electrodes and whose length, the lead’s strength, depends on the shape of the body and the conductivity of its tissues. The voltage in a lead is then the projection of the heart vector on the lead vector, times the lead vector’s length. Signal strength also falls as an electrode moves farther from the heart.

How this site computes the twelve leads

In the model the heart vector is the sum of the current dipoles of every cell in the simulated heart, computed (chapter 02) from the transmembrane voltage on the heart’s surfaces, and expressed in the axes of the Frank vectorcardiogram: X toward the left, Y toward the feet and Z toward the back. Leads I, II and V1 to V6 are weighted sums of X, Y and Z with the coefficients of the Dower matrix, and each row of the matrix is a lead vector. Dower reported that the ECG he derived from the Frank signals was close enough to the recorded one for serial comparisons to be valid. In one comparison of three methods for synthesizing a vectorcardiogram from a 12-lead ECG, the inverse of his matrix gave the most Frank-like QRS loops; a later comparison found Kors’s regression transformation more accurate for the X and Y leads. Leads III, aVR, aVL and aVF are then derived from I and II, as an electrocardiograph derives them. The model treats the limb electrodes, far from the heart, as seeing one central dipole. The chest electrodes sit close to it, where nearer muscle counts for more, so for V1 to V6 the model adds a near-field term: for each region of the simulated heart, the difference between its dipole seen from where the region lies and seen from the centre, scaled by a single strength used in every chapter. The near-field term is a modelling choice; it does not come from a measured torso. A 12-lead ECG synthesized from a vector approximates a recorded one but does not duplicate it.

Reading the figure

The drawing of the body marks the selected lead’s positive electrode and the electrode or terminal it is measured against. The hexaxial wheel is the frontal plane as the limb leads see it. Its arrow is the frontal heart vector rebuilt from leads I and aVF in Einthoven’s frame, so its shadow on any limb axis is proportional to that lead’s voltage, and equal to it for I, II and III. The blue band on the rim marks the normal axis range, the dark mark the mean QRS axis of this heart. The horizontal plane is seen from the feet, front of the chest at the top, with each chest lead along the direction of its Dower lead vector. In that plane the shadow is only the part of a chest lead that comes from the heart vector; in the enlarged tracing that part is drawn in grey, and the rest is the near-field term. Drag across a tracing to move through the beat, or pick a lead on either plane or on a tracing.

chapters.title: Recording
chapters.subtitle: Paper, filters, artifacts and cables
chapters.lede: The machine that records an electrocardiogram also shapes it. Paper speed and gain set the scales, the filters determine which frequencies pass, and every cable must reach the right electrode. Changing any of them can make a normal heart look abnormal.
chapters.body:
The paper

At 25 mm/s the standard page holds four 2.5-second columns, each the next 2.5 seconds of one continuous 10-second record. At normal standardization 10 mm equals 1 mV and 1 mm equals 0.1 mV. One small square, 1 mm, is therefore 40 ms across and 0.1 mV up. At 50 mm/s the same square is 20 ms, every complex is twice as wide and the page holds 5 seconds; at 20 mm/mV it is 0.05 mV and every complex is twice as tall. Speed and gain change how large the complexes are on paper; their durations and voltages stay the same. In the figure the calibration pulse at the start of each row is 1 mV high and 200 ms long, so its size shows the gain and speed in use. The leads, recorded together, must be aligned in time to within 10 ms.

Filters

The low-frequency cutoff (a high-pass filter) removes slow drift of the baseline; the high-frequency cutoff (a low-pass filter) removes fast noise. The recommended low-frequency cutoff is 0.05 Hz for routine filters, which may be relaxed to 0.67 Hz or below for linear digital filters with zero phase distortion. With traditional analog filtering, a 0.5 Hz cutoff introduces considerable distortion, particularly of the level of the ST segment. In the simulation the high-pass filter is a single resistor-capacitor stage run forward in time, as any analog circuit runs. After each large deflection it overshoots the other way, and the overshoot lands on the ST segment, moving it opposite to the QRS before it: up after the deep S of V2, down after the tall R of V5. Displacement of the ST segment is usually measured at its junction with the end of the QRS complex, the J point, and in some settings 40 to 80 ms after it; the ST card measures it 60 ms after the J point. A filter run a second time in reverse, a bidirectional filter, has zero phase shift; the zero-phase switch makes the high-pass and low-pass filters bidirectional. The high-frequency cutoff should be at least 150 Hz for adults and adolescents, and 500 samples per second are needed to allow it. The simulation produces one sample per millisecond. A 40 Hz cutoff invalidates any amplitude measurement used for diagnostic classification, so the machine should alert the user and restore the proper cutoff, and a 1 to 30 Hz band is unacceptable for diagnostic recording.

Artifacts

Low-frequency noise is baseline wander from respiration or movement; high-frequency noise is muscle artifact and power-line or radiated electromagnetic interference. The simulation adds each at the electrodes: a slow sway at one breath every 4 seconds, largest on the chest; random fast noise from the limb muscles that waxes and wanes; and a 60 Hz hum whose size differs from electrode to electrode. A lead records the difference between two potentials, so only the part of an artifact that differs between its electrodes reaches it. In the simulation the 0.5 Hz filter more than halves the wander, and when run forward it also shifts the ST segment. The 40 Hz filter removes most of the tremor, and amplitude measurements made through it are no longer valid for diagnostic classification.

Electrode placement

Limb electrodes belong on the arms and legs, distal to the shoulders and hips. Limb electrodes placed on the torso, as in the Mason-Likar position, give a tracing that is not equivalent to a standard electrocardiogram (ECG) for all purposes, must be labelled, and should not be compared serially with standard tracings; tracings taken sitting or upright are not equivalent to supine ones. V1 and V2 placed too high, in the second or third intercostal space, lose initial R amplitude, approximately 0.1 mV per interspace, which can mimic poor R-wave progression or anterior infarction, and may show an rSr′ complex with T-wave inversion that resembles aVR. V5 and V6 placed too low alter the voltages used to diagnose hypertrophy, and chest-electrode misplacement alters computer statements in up to 6% of recordings. The Dower matrix that turns the simulated heart vector into leads describes only the standard electrode positions, so misplaced electrodes are not simulated.

Cable reversals

Each electrode has its own cable: left arm (LA), right arm (RA), left leg (LL), right leg (RL) and V1 to V6. When only limb cables are interchanged, and the neutral (right leg) cable is not one of them, the leads are re-arranged, inverted or unchanged and the intervals stay the same. The clues are a negative P-QRS in lead I or II, a positive P-QRS in aVR, P-QRS complexes of opposite direction in I and V6, or a changed axis. Reversing the left and right arm cables inverts lead I, switches II with III and aVR with aVL, and leaves aVF and the chest leads unaltered; an important discordance between lead I and V6 distinguishes it from mirror-image dextrocardia. Reversing the right arm and right leg cables leaves very low amplitude only in lead II, with inverted symmetry between leads I and III. Reversing the left arm and left leg cables gives an often subtle shift in axis and inversion of lead III; changes in the P waves of the limb leads can raise the suspicion, although the specificity of that clue has been challenged. Reversing an arm cable and the neutral (right leg) cable distorts Wilson’s terminal, and so the chest and augmented leads; its telltale sign is an almost flat line in lead I, II or III. Reversing the two leg cables changes almost nothing, because the legs sit at nearly the same potential. Reversing the V1 and V2 cables can reverse R-wave progression and mimic anteroseptal infarction, and the P and T waves of those leads often progress abnormally too. A limb cable other than the neutral, reversed with a chest cable, distorts most leads and leaves at most one of I, II and III unchanged.

To reverse two cables, the simulation first recovers the potential under each electrode from the simulated leads, taking Wilson’s terminal as zero and the right leg at the left leg’s potential, because the potential difference between the two legs is nearly zero. It then lets the two cables trade electrodes and forms the twelve leads again, as a machine would. With the right leg at the left leg’s potential, lead II is exactly flat in the simulation when the right arm and right leg cables are reversed; in a patient it is nearly flat.
keypoints: Standard paper runs at 25 mm/s and 10 mm/mV, so one small square is 40 ms by 0.1 mV; read any other setting against the calibration pulse.
A diagnostic recording needs a low-frequency cutoff of 0.05 Hz (up to 0.67 Hz with zero-phase digital filters) and, in adults and adolescents, a high-frequency cutoff of at least 150 Hz.
An analog-style 0.5 Hz filter shifts the ST segment; a 40 Hz filter removes muscle noise but invalidates amplitude measurements used for diagnostic classification.
Left–right arm reversal inverts lead I, swaps II with III and aVR with aVL, and spares aVF and the chest leads; lead I and V6 then have QRS complexes of opposite direction.
An almost flat limb lead means the neutral (right leg) cable was involved; Wilson’s terminal, and every chest lead with it, is then distorted.

chapters.title: Activation
chapters.subtitle: The sequence of one heartbeat
chapters.lede: Each heartbeat is one wave of activation that starts in the sinus node and ends at the base of the ventricles, followed by a wave of recovery. The electrocardiogram (ECG) records where those waves are, millisecond by millisecond.
chapters.body:
The sinus node and the atria

The sinus node is a crescent of specialised cells, on average 13.5 mm long, lying under the epicardium where the superior vena cava meets the right atrium. Its discharge spreads through the right atrium and crosses to the left atrium mainly through Bachmann’s bundle. In 35 patients with a history of atrial fibrillation, mapped in sinus rhythm, the left atrium began to activate, in the region of Bachmann’s bundle, about 30 ms after the region of the sinus node. The P wave is the sum of that spread. Because the right atrium activates first and the left atrium last and posteriorly, the P wave in V1 is often biphasic. A P wave of 120 ms or more points to left atrial abnormality.

The atrioventricular (AV) node and the His–Purkinje system

The wave then reaches the AV node, which conducts slowly and so separates atrial from ventricular contraction. In the electrophysiology laboratory the interval from atrial activation at the node to the His bundle (AH) is normally about 55 to 125 ms, and from the His bundle to the first ventricular muscle (HV) 35 to 55 ms. Neither the AV node nor the His–Purkinje system has enough cells to produce a deflection at the body surface. The PR segment is level, but atrial recovery, a small wave opposite in sign to the P wave (the Ta wave), runs through it. The PR interval, from the start of the P wave to the start of the QRS, is normally 120 to 200 ms. Below 120 ms, with a delta wave and a wide QRS, it suggests pre-excitation; above 200 ms is first-degree AV block. In this simulated heart the wave reaches the AV node 90 ms after the sinus node fires and leaves it 34 ms later, before the last atrial cell activates at 141 ms. That AV nodal delay is shorter than in most people, below the normal AH range, and the level PR segment here is the time the wave spends in the His–Purkinje system.

The ventricles: the QRS

In isolated human hearts, three endocardial areas of the left ventricle activate first, within 5 ms of each other: an anterior paraseptal area just below the mitral valve, a posterior paraseptal area a third of the way from apex to base, and the centre of the left septal surface; the right ventricle begins 5 to 10 ms later, near the anterior papillary muscle. The septum is therefore activated from left to right first, a small vector toward the right and front that produces the septal q wave in I, aVL, V5 and V6 and the small r in V1. In this simulated heart the first force points more upward than to the right, so its septal q waves fall in II, III, aVF, V5 and V6 rather than in I and aVL. The wave then spreads through the Purkinje network along the endocardium, much faster than it crosses the wall, and the left ventricle, with the most muscle, dominates the QRS. The last regions are the posterior base of the left ventricle and the right ventricular outflow tract. In the simulated heart the apical tip activates nearly as late as the base, because the fast endocardial layer that stands in for the Purkinje network stops short of it. In adults a QRS longer than 110 ms is abnormal.

The plateau and recovery: the ST segment and the T wave

Each ventricular cell holds its plateau for about 200 ms, and for a time all of them are on it at once: in the simulated heart, for about 140 ms after the last cell activates. Neighbours then differ little in voltage, little current flows, and the ST segment lies near the baseline; in V2 and V3 of men, 1 to 2 mm above it can be a normal finding. Recovery follows a different order from activation. In human hearts the regions activated earliest have the longest action potentials, and recovery gradients run along all axes of the ventricles. The result is a T wave that, in most leads, points the same way as the QRS. Its size reflects how spread out in time the recovery is across the heart’s surfaces. The QT interval spans activation and recovery together; corrected for rate, 450 ms or more in men and 460 ms or more in women is prolonged.

The simulated heart and the heart vector

The heart on the left is the simulated heart from which every tracing on this site is computed. Colour marks muscle that has activated, from early (pale rose) to late (deep indigo), with a white line every 10 ms; muscle that has recovered turns pale blue. The lines inside it are the conduction system. They turn coral as the simulated impulse passes, and a bright point marks where the impulse is. The Inside the heart button at the top of the page plays the same beat up to 16 times slower than life, with a ladder diagram under the tracing. The arrow is the heart vector, the sum of every cell’s current at that instant, and its trail is the vectorcardiographic loop. Each limb lead on the right records that same arrow from its own direction; the chest leads, close to the heart, also see nearby regions more strongly (chapter 03).
keypoints: The P wave is atrial activation. The PR segment spans the AV node and His–Purkinje system, which produce no deflection, while atrial recovery runs through it. The QRS is ventricular activation, the ST segment the plateau, and the T wave recovery.

The septum activates first, from left to right, which produces the septal q wave in I, aVL, V5 and V6 and the r in V1. The simulated heart’s first force points more upward than to the right, so its q waves are in II, III, aVF, V5 and V6.
Activation runs fast along the endocardium and slowly across the wall; the left ventricle dominates the QRS.
A nearly level ST segment means every cell is on its plateau and neighbours differ little in voltage, so little current flows.

Earlier-activated regions have longer action potentials, so recovery is spread over a narrower span than activation; with gradients along every axis, the T wave points the same way as the QRS in most leads.

chapters.title: Waves and intervals
chapters.subtitle: Measuring the beat, and the heart rate
chapters.lede: The electrocardiogram (ECG) is read as waves, the level segments between them, and intervals that span both. Each wave and segment is a stretch of time on the paper that matches one step of the beat; an interval spans more than one.
chapters.body:
Waves, segments and intervals

A wave is a deflection from the baseline; a segment is the level line between two waves; an interval spans at least one wave. The P wave is atrial activation. The PR interval runs from the start of the P wave to the start of the QRS complex, so it includes atrial activation and the conduction through the atrioventricular (AV) node and the His–Purkinje system; its level part after the P wave is the PR segment. The QRS complex is ventricular activation. Its end is the J point, where the ST segment begins; the ST segment runs to the start of the T wave, the recovery of the ventricles. The QT interval runs from the onset of the QRS, the earliest sign of ventricular depolarization, to the end of the T wave, the latest sign of repolarization. The TP segment, from the end of the T wave to the next P wave, is the resting baseline, and the RR interval is the time from one R wave to the next. A U wave, when present, follows the T wave and is most evident in V2 and V3; the normal simulated heart produces none, and chapter 21 adds a stand-in U wave for hypokalemia.

Measuring on paper

At the standard paper speed of 25 mm/s, each 1 mm small box is 40 ms and each 5 mm large box is 200 ms; at the standard gain, 10 mm is 1 mV. An interval is read with calipers or by counting boxes. Where a wave starts and ends depends on the lead: in a lead nearly perpendicular to the first or last forces of a wave, the wave looks shorter. Electrocardiographs that record all leads at once can align them, and their QT is often longer than the QT measured in any single lead. The cards give intervals timed from the simulated cells. The PR interval runs from the moment the sinus node fires to the first ventricular cell to activate, the QRS from the first ventricular cell to activate to the last, and the QT from the first to activate to the last to recover. Measured on the tracing, the P wave and PR interval are slightly shorter, because the cells at either end of atrial activation produce almost no signal. The P-wave calipers are therefore set on the tracing, as chapter 16 measures it: from the first to the last moment the P wave is 0.01 mV or more from the baseline in any lead. Calipers on lead II alone can give a shorter value; drag them on the figure to try it.

Normal values in adults

A PR interval above 200 ms is first-degree AV block. A PR interval below 120 ms, with a delta wave and a wide QRS, suggests pre-excitation. A QRS longer than 110 ms is abnormal. With the pattern of a bundle branch block, 120 ms or more is complete block and 110 to 119 ms is incomplete block; the 2009 statement gives 110 to 120 ms for incomplete right bundle branch block. The 2009 recommendations give no normal duration for the P wave; a P wave of 120 ms or more points to left atrial abnormality. The simulated P wave is smaller than in most people: about 0.046 mV above the baseline before it in lead II, against 0.070 mV for the median of the real normal ECGs it was fitted to. The QT shortens as the rate rises, so it is judged after correction for rate (chapter 08): a corrected QT of 450 ms or more in men, or 460 ms or more in women, is prolonged.

Heart rate

In normal adults the resting sinus rate is generally between 50 and 90 per minute; sinus tachycardia is a sinus rate above 100 per minute. The bradycardia guideline uses a sinus rate below 50 per minute, and notes that the National Institutes of Health uses 60. The ways of counting follow from the paper speed. For a regular rhythm, divide 300 by the number of large boxes between two R waves, or 1500 by the number of small boxes. When an R wave falls on a heavy line, the next heavy lines read 300, 150, 100, 75, 60 and 50, and the next R wave is read off where it lands. For an irregular rhythm, count the QRS complexes in 6 seconds (30 large boxes) and multiply by 10. Because that count moves in steps of 10 per minute, it is coarse for a regular rhythm; the strip shows both methods side by side. The simulated PR interval stays at 170 ms at every rate on the slider.
keypoints: Waves are deflections, segments are the level lines between them, and intervals span both: the PR interval contains the P wave, the QT interval the QRS and the T wave.
At 25 mm/s a small box is 40 ms and a large box 200 ms; at 10 mm/mV a small box is 0.1 mV<cite data-ref="kligfield2007,hancock2009"></cite>.
The PR interval is atrial activation plus the delay in the AV node and His–Purkinje system; above 200 ms is first-degree AV block<cite data-ref="kusumoto2019"></cite>.
A QRS longer than 110 ms is abnormal, and 120 ms or more with a bundle branch pattern is complete block<cite data-ref="surawicz2009"></cite>.
Rate is 300 divided by the large boxes, or 1500 by the small boxes, between R waves; for an irregular rhythm, count the QRS complexes in 6 seconds and multiply by 10.

chapters.title: Axis
chapters.subtitle: The direction of the QRS in the frontal plane
chapters.lede: The six limb leads view the heart vector from six directions in the frontal plane. The mean direction of the QRS in that plane, its axis, depends on the heart’s position in the chest and on the order in which the left ventricle (LV) activates.
chapters.body:
The hexaxial reference

Leads I, II and III and the augmented leads aVR, aVL and aVF all lie in the frontal plane. The six are computed from two measured signals, so they are six views of one frontal vector. Drawn through one centre, their axes are 30° apart: lead I points to the patient’s left at 0°, aVF to the feet at +90°, II at +60°, III at +120°, aVL at −30° and aVR at −150°; angles above the horizontal are negative. A lead records a positive QRS when the QRS forces point toward its positive pole, a negative QRS when they point away, and an equiphasic (isoelectric) QRS when they are perpendicular to it. In the Cabrera sequence, aVL, I, −aVR, II, aVF, III, the limb leads follow one another around the circle, which makes the axis easier to read.

Reading the axis

The 2009 recommendations define the mean frontal axis by the dominant QRS deflection. The axis in the cards is computed from the net area of the QRS in leads I and aVF. At the bedside it can be estimated in four steps:

  1. Lead I: a net positive QRS puts the axis in the left half of the circle, between −90° and +90°.
  2. Lead aVF: a net positive QRS puts it in the lower half, between 0° and 180°. If both are positive, the axis lies between 0° and +90°.
  3. If I is positive and aVF negative, look at lead II. Positive places the axis between −30° and 0°, which is still normal; negative places it beyond −30°, left axis deviation.
  4. Find the limb lead whose QRS is most nearly isoelectric. The axis lies about 90° from it, on the side where the QRS is positive.

Normal and abnormal axes

In adults the normal axis lies between −30° and +90°. Left axis deviation (LAD) is moderate from −30° to −45° and marked from −45° to −90°, which is often associated with left anterior fascicular block (LAFB). Right axis deviation (RAD) is moderate from +90° to +120° and marked from +120° to 180°, which is often associated with left posterior fascicular block (LPFB). With an equiphasic QRS the axis is indeterminate. The statement’s text calls −30° itself left axis deviation, while its table begins left axis deviation below −30°; the cards and the wheel follow the table. The adult table gives no range for axes between −90° and ±180° through −135°, the upper left of the wheel (up and toward the patient’s right); the diagnostic statement list of the same series names such an axis right superior axis, without giving a range. The axis depends on age and body habitus, and shifts to the left with age.

What moves the axis

The heart’s position. In 185 healthy adults the long axis of the left ventricle pointed about 50° from straight ahead toward the left, seen from above, and about 29° below the horizontal once its three plane angles are combined (36° in the view from the front); it lay flatter in people with a larger chest circumference. Tilting the simulated apex toward the feet swings the QRS axis toward +90°. Rotating the heart about its long axis also moves it, because the rotation changes which walls face the left arm and the feet. The simulated heart’s position was fitted to median electrocardiograms (ECGs) of normal recordings, not to anatomy, and the fit left its long axis flatter than the anatomical mean: 21° below the horizontal against about 29°. The preset “Anatomical mean” sets that direction. The study of 185 adults also measured a second axis, which fixes the rotation, but it scattered widely (standard deviations of 17° to 32°), so the preset leaves the rotation at zero.

The order of activation. When the left anterior fascicle is blocked, the anterior and superior wall of the left ventricle activates last and the axis moves to between −45° and −90°, with qR in aVL and rS in II, III and aVF. A left posterior fascicular block moves it to between +90° and 180°, with rS in I and aVL and qR in III and aVF. Neither block was used to fit the simulation; the cards show whether the simulated axis reaches the criteria. At the fitted position the simulated blocks reach (LAFB) or approach (LPFB) the axis criterion but not the QRS patterns: in LAFB the inferior leads keep tall R waves and aVL begins with a deep Q; in LPFB lead I has no S wave, and III and aVF begin with deep Q waves. Right ventricular (RV) hypertrophy also turns the axis rightward, and right axis deviation, with prominent anterior forces in the right precordial leads, should be required for that diagnosis in nearly all cases. Left bundle branch block can move the axis to the right, to the left or upward.

The P and T axes

The same construction gives an axis for the P wave and for the T wave. In adults the T wave is upright in I and II and inverted in aVR, so its axis, like the QRS axis, points down and to the left. The angle between the QRS and T axes in the frontal plane has no agreed cutoff. In three dimensions, the spatial QRS-T angle is the angle between the mean QRS and T vectors computed from the X, Y and Z leads. In the Rotterdam Study of adults aged 55 and over it was graded normal from 0° to 105°, borderline from 105° to 135° and abnormal from 135° to 180°, and an abnormal angle had an age- and sex-adjusted hazard ratio of 5.2 for cardiac death. In the simulation each cell keeps the action potential duration it has in the normal beat, so a block that changes the order of activation changes the order of recovery with it (a secondary repolarization change), and a fascicular block widens the angle.
keypoints: The six limb leads view one frontal vector from directions 30° apart. A lead is positive when the QRS forces point toward its positive pole and isoelectric when they are perpendicular to it.
Lead I and aVF both positive put the axis between 0° and +90°. When aVF is negative, a positive lead II keeps the axis within the normal range.
The adult normal axis is −30° to +90°; beyond −30° is left axis deviation and beyond +90° right axis deviation<cite data-ref="surawicz2009"></cite>.
The axis follows the heart’s position in the chest and the order of activation: LAFB moves it to between −45° and −90°, LPFB to between +90° and 180°<cite data-ref="surawicz2009"></cite>.
The spatial QRS-T angle, from the mean QRS and T vectors, is normal up to 105° and abnormal from 135°<cite data-ref="kardys2003"></cite>.

chapters.title: Repolarization and the QT interval
chapters.subtitle: The T wave, the QT and its correction for rate
chapters.lede: The T wave is the ventricles recovering, and the QT interval spans their activation and recovery. Recovery shortens as the heart rate rises, so the QT is corrected for rate; the corrected value depends on the formula used.
chapters.body:
Where the T wave comes from

After its upstroke each ventricular cell holds a plateau, then repolarizes. While every cell is on its plateau, neighbours differ little in voltage, little current flows between them and the ST segment is nearly level; the T wave arises as cells recover at different times, and its amplitude is proportional to how widely recovery times are spread over the surfaces of the ventricles. The QT interval runs from the onset of the QRS, the earliest sign of ventricular depolarization, to the end of the T wave, the latest sign of repolarization. In human hearts the regions activated earliest have the longest action potentials, and repolarization gradients run along every axis of the ventricles. In the simulation, each cell’s activation-recovery interval (ARI, from its activation to 50% repolarization) is a straight-line function of when that cell activates in the normal beat, with a slope of −0.59 after fitting; one published model uses −0.66. The model also includes small gradients across the wall, from apex to base and between the ventricles. With the −0.59 slope and these gradients, the cells pass the midpoint of recovery within a narrower span than they activate (the ribbons under the tracing), and that span lies under the peak of the T wave. Each cell also repolarizes gradually, over about 100 ms from 90% to 10% of its plateau in the model, and this spreads the T wave on either side.

Measuring the QT

The QT is measured in the lead where it is longest, usually V2 or V3; a value more than 40 ms longer than in the other leads may be an error. Where the T and U waves merge, the QT is measured in leads without U waves, often aVR and aVL, or the end of the T wave is found by the tangent method: a tangent to the steepest part of the T wave’s downslope, extended until it crosses the baseline. Both may underestimate the QT. In the simulation the tangent meets the baseline before the last cell has recovered, because the last, slow part of recovery barely deflects the tracing. In this simulated heart the longest tangent QT is usually in V5 or V6, partly because every lead here is timed from the same QRS onset; on a real tracing the QRS starts up to 20 ms earlier in V2 and V3. The bars give the tangent QT in every lead. The 2009 statement on the QT interval calls a T wave flat when its peak lies between +0.1 and −0.1 mV in leads I, II, aVL (with an R wave taller than 0.3 mV) and V4 to V6; the bars grey out a T wave this small in any lead, because a tangent drawn on so small a wave is unreliable.

Correcting for rate

The QT shortens as the heart rate rises. In the simulation every cell’s ARI scales with the cube root of the RR interval. The cube root was chosen for the model rather than measured, and the simulated QT–RR relation follows from it. A corrected QT (QTc) estimates the QT at 60 per minute, an RR of 1 s, and every formula returns the measured QT unchanged at that rate. With QT and RR in seconds:

  • Bazett: QT/√RR, derived in 1920 from 39 young subjects.
  • Fridericia: QT/∛RR.
  • Framingham: QT + 0.154 (1 − RR), from 5,018 people with heart rates of 41 to 120 per minute.
  • Hodges: QT + 1.75 ms × (heart rate − 60), with the heart rate per minute. The 1983 original is a meeting abstract that is not indexed; the formula here is as given by Vandenberk and colleagues in their 2018 correction.

Bazett’s formula “overcorrects the QT interval at fast heart rates and undercorrects it at low heart rates”. It leaves a positive correlation of the QTc with heart rate (r = 0.32), and Fridericia’s a negative one (r = −0.26 to −0.32). In 6,609 hospital patients in sinus rhythm with a normal QRS and heart rates below 90 per minute, the slope of the QTc against RR was 0.004 for Fridericia, −0.005 for Framingham and −0.071 for Bazett; a prolonged QTc had a hazard ratio for death within 30 days of 7.31 by Framingham, 5.95 by Fridericia and 4.49 by Bazett. The 2009 statement advises linear regression formulas rather than Bazett’s, naming the method in the report, and no rate correction when the RR varies widely, as in atrial fibrillation. In the chart, a perfect formula for this heart would plot as a flat line at its QT at 60 per minute.

Thresholds

In adults a QTc of 450 ms or more in men, or 460 ms or more in women, is prolonged, and 390 ms or less is short. The 2009 statement’s text gives the men’s limit as “longer than 450 ms”; its recommendation, followed here, says 450 ms or longer. In Drew and colleagues’ 2010 statement, the 99th percentile is about 470 ms in men and 480 ms in women, and a QTc above 500 ms is highly abnormal; data from congenital long-QT syndrome tie it to a two- to threefold higher risk of torsade de pointes (TdP). The same statement defines a prolonged QTc differently, as one above the 99th percentile. On a drug that can cause TdP, prompt action is indicated if the QTc exceeds 500 ms or rises by at least 60 ms from its value before the drug. Limits depend on the formula: with Bazett’s, the 99% upper limits were 472 ms in men and 482 ms in women.
keypoints: The T wave arises as ventricular cells recover at different times; the QT runs from the first sign of activation to the last sign of recovery.

Measure the QT in the lead where it is longest, usually V2 or V3; the tangent method finds the end of the T wave where U waves interfere, and can underestimate the QT<cite data-ref="rautaharju2009"></cite>.
Every formula returns the QT unchanged at 60 per minute. Bazett’s over-corrects at fast rates and under-corrects at slow ones<cite data-ref="sagie1992"></cite>.
A QTc of 450 ms or more in men, or 460 ms or more in women, is prolonged; above 500 ms is highly abnormal<cite data-ref="rautaharju2009,drew2010"></cite>.
On a drug that can cause torsade de pointes, a QTc above 500 ms or a rise of 60 ms or more calls for prompt action<cite data-ref="drew2010"></cite>.

chapters.title: Sinus rhythm
chapters.subtitle: The sinus node and its rate
chapters.lede: The sinus node is the heart’s normal pacemaker. In sinus rhythm every P wave comes from it, so every P wave has the same shape; the rate, its swing with breathing and any pause are read from the spacing of those P waves.
chapters.body:
The sinus P wave and the resting rate

The sinus node fires spontaneously, and each discharge spreads across the atria, producing a P wave. In sinus rhythm every P wave comes from that node, so every P wave has the same shape: upright in leads I, II and aVF and biphasic in V1. Each is followed by a QRS complex after the same PR interval. In normal people at rest the sinus rate is generally between 50 and 90 beats per minute (bpm), reflecting vagal tone.

Bradycardia and tachycardia

The 2018 bradycardia guideline defines sinus bradycardia as a sinus rate below 50 bpm. It notes that the National Institutes of Health (NIH) uses 60 bpm instead, and that in population studies the lowest second percentile of heart rate ranged from 40 to 55 bpm, depending on age and sex. With rare exceptions, the guideline considers treating sinus node dysfunction only when it causes symptoms. Sinus tachycardia is a sinus rate above 100 bpm. It is physiological as a response to exercise or emotion, and it also follows fever, dehydration, anemia, heart failure, hyperthyroidism, caffeine, beta-agonist drugs and stimulants. In patients, activation arises from higher in the right atrium as the sinus rate rises, which makes the P wave taller in the inferior leads. The simulated node always fires from one site, so its P wave keeps one shape at every rate.

Sinus arrhythmia

Sinus arrhythmia, one of the standard statements of the American Heart Association (AHA) electrocardiogram (ECG) lexicon, is sinus rhythm whose rate varies from beat to beat. In the simulation the sinus interval swings with a 4-second breathing cycle, shorter and then longer. Because every beat still starts in the sinus node, each P wave keeps its shape and the PR interval stays the same.

Sinus pause

In the 2018 guideline a sinus pause means that the sinus node depolarizes more than 3 s after the last atrial depolarization; sinus node arrest means no evidence of sinus node depolarization at all. Pauses of 2 s in healthy elderly people and of 3 s in long-distance runners have been recorded on 24-hour monitoring, and the guideline warns that a pause over 3 s, or a rate below 50 bpm, should not by itself be used to diagnose sinus node dysfunction. When the sinus node is slow, a subsidiary pacemaker (an ectopic atrial focus, the atrioventricular (AV) junction or the ventricles) can take over. In the simulated pause the node skips its discharges, so there is no P wave and no QRS, and no escape beat is simulated.

Reading the ladder

Under the strip is a ladder diagram, the timing chart drawn to reason about a rhythm. Its tiers are the atria (A), the AV node with the His bundle (AV), and the ventricles (V); time runs left to right on the same axis as the strip. Each line is one wave crossing one tier, drawn at the times the simulation computed. In sinus rhythm a line starts at the top of the atrial tier, where the sinus node is; crosses the AV tier slowly, during the second half of the P wave and the flat PR segment; and crosses the ventricular tier quickly, during the QRS. A pause is an empty stretch in all three tiers.

How the beats are simulated

Each beat is computed by the activation model: the P wave from the sinus node through the simulated atria, and the QRS and T wave from the His bundle, with recovery set by the interval before each beat so that the QT follows the rate. The simulated P wave is smaller than in most people: about 0.046 mV above baseline in lead II, against 0.070 mV for the median of the real normal ECGs it was fitted to. At the strip's 10 mm/mV it is less than half a millimetre tall, so the P-wave panel draws it at twice that gain.
keypoints: In sinus rhythm every P wave comes from the sinus node: upright in I, II and aVF, biphasic in V1, and the same from beat to beat.
Sinus bradycardia is a sinus rate below 50 bpm in the 2018 guideline (below 60 bpm by the NIH definition); sinus tachycardia is a sinus rate above 100 bpm.
In sinus arrhythmia only the spacing of the P waves changes; their shape and the PR interval do not.
A sinus pause is more than 3 s from one atrial depolarization to the next; on its own it does not establish sinus node dysfunction.
A ladder diagram plots each wave through the atria, the AV node and the ventricles on the same time axis as the strip.

chapters.title: Atrial arrhythmias
chapters.subtitle: When the atria are not driven by the sinus node
chapters.lede: When something other than the sinus node drives the atria, the P wave changes shape or gives way to flutter or fibrillatory waves, and the rhythm changes pace. A premature atrial complex (PAC) is a single early beat. In focal atrial tachycardia (AT) one focus fires fast and steadily, in multifocal atrial tachycardia (MAT) several foci compete, in atrial flutter a wave travels continuously around a re-entrant circuit, and in atrial fibrillation (AF) there is no organized atrial activity at all.
chapters.body:
Premature atrial complexes

A premature atrial complex (PAC) is an atrial beat that comes before the next sinus beat is due, from a site other than the sinus node. Because it starts elsewhere its P wave has a different shape, and an early one may land on the preceding T wave. A PAC early enough to find the atrioventricular (AV) node still refractory is not conducted: the American Heart Association (AHA) lexicon lists these as nonconducted atrial premature complexes. Atrial fibrillation (AF) is frequently initiated after PACs, and a higher PAC burden is associated with developing AF. In the simulation the PAC's wave also reaches the sinus node and resets it, so the next sinus beat comes one sinus cycle after the wave arrives there.

Focal atrial tachycardia

Focal atrial tachycardia (AT) arises from a localized atrial site, with regular, organized atrial activity, discrete P waves and, typically, an isoelectric segment between them; the 2023 AF guideline describes it as a regular atrial rhythm at a constant rate above 100 beats per minute (bpm), activated from outside the sinus node. The atrial rate is usually between 100 and 250 bpm, and irregularity is sometimes seen at onset (a warm-up). The P wave points to the focus: a positive P in V1 with negative P waves in I and aVL suggests a left atrial origin, and positive P waves in II, III and aVF an origin high in either atrium. The P waves of the simulated foci follow from the model's atrial geometry, so they need not match these rules exactly. Because the atria drive the rhythm and conduct normally to the ventricles, the P wave usually sits closer to the next QRS than to the previous one, so the RP interval, from the onset of the QRS to the onset of the P wave after it, is long.

Multifocal atrial tachycardia

Multifocal atrial tachycardia (MAT) is a rapid, irregular rhythm with at least three distinct P-wave morphologies on the surface electrocardiogram (ECG). The atrial rate is above 100 bpm (above 90 bpm in at least one report), there is a distinct isoelectric period between P waves, and the PP, PR and RR intervals vary. It can be hard to tell from AF at the bedside or even on a single tracing. In the simulation four origins take turns at irregular intervals; the PR interval varies because each origin is a different distance from the AV node and because the simulated node conducts an early impulse more slowly. The simulated P wave is smaller than in most people: about 0.046 mV above baseline in lead II, against 0.070 mV for the median of the real normal ECGs it was fitted to. The shapes are therefore easier to compare in the P-wave panel, which draws them aligned at onset and at twice the strip's gain.

Atrial fibrillation

In AF atrial activation is uncoordinated and atrial contraction ineffective. Its ECG features are irregular RR intervals (when AV conduction is present), the absence of distinct P waves, and irregular atrial activity, the fibrillatory waves; the diagnosis always requires visual confirmation. AF that terminates within 7 days of onset is paroxysmal; persistent AF is continuous for more than 7 days and requires intervention; long-standing persistent AF is continuous for more than 12 months. In the simulation the AV node passes impulses at random intervals, never sooner than its recovery allows, so no two RR intervals match.

Atrial flutter

Typical atrial flutter is a macroreentrant circuit around the tricuspid annulus through the cavotricuspid isthmus. Running counterclockwise it produces predominantly negative sawtooth flutter waves in II, III and aVF and a positive deflection in V1; running clockwise (reverse typical flutter) it produces positive flutter waves inferiorly and wide negative ones in V1. The typical atrial rate is 300 bpm, a cycle length of 200 ms, and it can be slower with antiarrhythmic drugs or atrial scarring. The 2015 supraventricular tachycardia guideline gives the range as 250 to 350 bpm in one passage and as typically 250 to 330 bpm in another. The AV node passes only some flutter waves; at 2:1 conduction the ventricles follow every second one. An atrial rate above the ventricular rate usually means atrial flutter or atrial tachycardia, and flutter with variable conduction makes the ventricular rate irregular.

How each rhythm is simulated

Premature beats, focal AT and MAT are computed by the activation model: each P wave is the simulated atria activating from its origin, so its shape follows from where that origin is. The activation model has no reentry, so fibrillatory and flutter waves come from a phenomenological atrial signal, one that imitates the waves without simulating atrial cells. For fibrillation the signal is a random atrial vector and for flutter a rotating one. It is added to simulated ventricular beats, and its lines in the ladder are dashed. The AV node's refractoriness and its slower conduction of early impulses follow a simple timing rule rather than a model of the node.
keypoints: A premature atrial complex is an early P wave of a different shape; a very early one can find the AV node refractory and not conduct.
Focal AT: regular, discrete P waves of one non-sinus shape, usually 100 to 250 bpm, typically with a long RP; the P wave’s shape points to the focus.
Multifocal AT: at least three P-wave shapes, an irregular rhythm above 100 bpm, and an isoelectric baseline between P waves.
AF: irregular RR intervals, no distinct P waves, and fibrillatory waves.
Typical flutter produces negative sawtooth waves in II, III and aVF and a positive deflection in V1, typically at 300 bpm; the conduction ratio sets the ventricular rate.

chapters.title: Re-entrant supraventricular tachycardia (SVT)
chapters.subtitle: Circuits through the atrioventricular node and accessory pathways
chapters.lede: In a re-entrant tachycardia one impulse keeps travelling around a loop, down one path and back up another, re-exciting the tissue it has just left. The route of the loop determines where the P wave falls and whether the QRS is narrow or wide.
chapters.body:
Re-entry above the ventricles

Supraventricular tachycardia (SVT) is an umbrella term for tachycardias with atrial or ventricular rates above 100 beats per minute (bpm) at rest whose mechanism involves tissue from the His bundle upward; in the 2015 guideline it does not include atrial fibrillation. Paroxysmal SVT, regular and rapid with abrupt onset and termination, is characteristic of atrioventricular (AV) nodal re-entrant tachycardia (AVNRT) and AV re-entrant tachycardia (AVRT), and less often of atrial tachycardia. AVNRT and AVRT are both re-entrant: an impulse travels down one limb of a circuit and returns up another, so it keeps re-exciting the tissue it has just left.

Typical AV nodal re-entry

AVNRT uses two functionally distinct pathways: a fast one, most commonly near the apex of Koch's triangle, and a slow one inferoposterior to the compact AV node. Koch's triangle is the area of the right atrium where the AV node connects with the atrium; its apex, where the fast pathway's connections lie, is close to the His bundle. In typical (slow–fast) AVNRT the impulse goes down the slow pathway and back up the fast pathway. From the bottom of the circuit the wave reaches the His bundle and the atria at about the same time, so atrial activation is nearly simultaneous with the QRS. The P wave is hidden in it except for its end, which appears at the end of the QRS as a narrow negative deflection in the inferior leads (a pseudo-S wave) and a slightly positive one in V1 (a pseudo-R′). The ventricular rate is often 180 to 200 bpm, with a range of 110 to more than 250 bpm. The simulation reproduces a small pseudo-S, about 0.03 mV deep in lead II. It does not reproduce the pseudo-R′: the simulated atria are activated from the AV junction, and their retrograde P wave is negative in V1 as well, so in V1 the end of the S wave deepens instead.

AV re-entry over an accessory pathway

An accessory pathway is an extranodal connection between atrial and ventricular muscle across the AV groove; one that conducts only retrogradely is concealed and leaves the electrocardiogram (ECG) in sinus rhythm unchanged. In orthodromic AVRT the impulse goes down the AV node and the His–Purkinje system, through the ventricles, and back up the pathway to the atria. The ventricles must be activated as far as the pathway before the atria can be, so the retrograde P wave comes after the QRS, usually in the early part of the ST–T segment, and the QRS is narrow unless there is bundle branch block or aberrant conduction. In antidromic AVRT the circuit runs the other way, down the pathway and back up through the AV node, and the QRS is wide, maximally pre-excited. A wide-complex tachycardia (QRS over 120 ms) may be ventricular tachycardia or a supraventricular rhythm with abnormal conduction, including conduction over an accessory pathway.

The RP interval

The RP interval runs from the onset of the QRS to the onset of the visible P wave. When the P wave lies closer to the preceding QRS than to the next one, the tachycardia has a short RP: typical AVNRT and orthodromic AVRT are short-RP tachycardias, with one P wave for each QRS. The RP is long when the impulse returns to the atria slowly: in atypical (fast–slow) AVNRT, where it goes back up a slow pathway, and in the permanent form of junctional reciprocating tachycardia (PJRT), an orthodromic AVRT over a slowly conducting, usually posteroseptal, concealed pathway, with deeply inverted P waves in II, III and aVF. Focal atrial tachycardia usually has a long RP, because the atria drive the rhythm and conduct normally to the ventricles. The guideline's diagnostic algorithm uses an RP of 90 ms measured on the surface ECG, distinct from the 70-ms ventriculoatrial interval used inside the heart.

How the circuits are built

In the simulation each tachycardia is a timed sequence of atrial and ventricular activations. Every atrial activation starts from the cell where the impulse enters the atria (the AV junction, or the atrial end of the pathway), and the model computes its P wave from the spread of activation; every ventricular activation starts at the His bundle or at the pathway's ventricular end. The model also computes how long the wave takes to travel from the pathway to the AV node, from the His bundle to the pathway, and from the pathway's insertion to the His–Purkinje system. The delays inside the circuit, such as how long the slow pathway or the AV node takes, are set so the cycle matches the chosen rate; they are not measured. In orthodromic AVRT the time the impulse takes to cross the accessory pathway back to the atria is also set by hand, at 50 ms, so that the P wave starts after the QRS, in the early part of the ST–T segment, as the guideline describes. In the enlarged view the grey trace is the same QRS and T wave without the atria, so the gap between the two lines is the retrograde P wave. The simulated P wave is smaller than in most people: about 0.046 mV above baseline in lead II, against 0.070 mV for the median of the real normal ECGs it was fitted to.
keypoints: Typical AVNRT: down the slow pathway, back up the fast; atria and ventricles activate together, so the P wave hides in the QRS and shows only at its end (pseudo-S in II, III and aVF; pseudo-R′ in V1).
Orthodromic AVRT: down the AV node, back up an accessory pathway; the retrograde P wave falls in the early ST–T segment and the QRS is narrow.
Antidromic AVRT: down the pathway, back up the AV node; the QRS is wide and maximally pre-excited.
Short RP (the P wave closer to the preceding QRS): typical AVNRT and orthodromic AVRT. Long RP: atypical AVNRT, PJRT and, usually, focal atrial tachycardia.
A ladder diagram shows each limb of a circuit: where the impulse goes down, and where it comes back up.

chapters.title: Ventricular arrhythmias
chapters.subtitle: Beats and rhythms that start in the ventricles
chapters.lede: A beat that starts in ventricular muscle spreads from one point without the conduction system. Its QRS is wide, and its direction shows where it began. A run of such beats is ventricular tachycardia, and disorganized ventricular activity is ventricular fibrillation.
chapters.body:
Beats that start in the ventricles

A premature ventricular complex (PVC) starts in ventricular muscle before the next sinus beat is due. It does not use the His–Purkinje system, so the wave spreads more slowly, from its origin through working muscle. The QRS is wide, and the ST segment and T wave point away from it. In the simulation the sinus node is not reset: its next P wave comes on time, finds the atrioventricular (AV) node refractory and is not conducted, so the pause after the PVC is fully compensatory. PVCs are called frequent when there is at least one on a 12-lead electrocardiogram (ECG) or more than 30 per hour, and more than 10,000 to 20,000 a day can cause a PVC-induced cardiomyopathy. The simulated PVCs are 165 to 224 ms wide, depending on the origin. That is wider than in one series of 45 patients with frequent PVCs and no structural heart disease, where they measured 142 ms in those whose left ventricle stayed normal and 159 ms in those who developed that cardiomyopathy. In the model a fast layer represents the Purkinje network, and a wave that starts in the muscle crosses that layer no faster than it crosses muscle, which widens the QRS. The strip can also show a PVC after every sinus beat (bigeminy) or PVCs in pairs (couplets).

Reading the origin from the QRS

The QRS of an ectopic beat points from where the wave starts toward the muscle it reaches last, so the origin can be read mainly from two groups of leads. The inferior leads (II, III, aVF) separate high from low: a focus in an outflow tract, at the top of the ventricles, sends the wave down toward the apex, and the QRS is positive in II, III and aVF; a focus at the apex or in the inferior wall sends it upward, and they are negative. V1, over the right ventricle (RV), separates right from left: a focus in the RV activates the left ventricle (LV) last, leftward and back, away from V1, so V1 is mainly negative, as in left bundle branch block (LBBB); a focus in the LV lateral wall activates the RV last, toward V1, and V1 is mainly positive, as in right bundle branch block (RBBB). The two outflow tracts are harder to tell apart: in patients, ventricular arrhythmias from the outflow tracts "usually exhibit either an RBBB or LBBB morphology with an inferior axis". The precordial transition is the first chest lead (V1 to V6, the precordial leads) in which the QRS is mainly positive; with an LBBB pattern, a transition after V3 indicates the RV outflow tract, and one by V3 could indicate a left-sided origin. In the simulated heart the RV outflow tract focus turns mainly positive only at V4, and the LV outflow tract focus is already mainly positive in V1. For a focus at the apex or in the inferior wall, V1 helps little in the simulated heart, and the other leads help more. Choose an origin and compare its QRS in II, III, aVF and V1 with these rules; the map shows when each part of the front of the heart activated. In patients, idiopathic ventricular arrhythmias most often arise from the RV outflow tract or the ostium of the LV, the opening to which the aorta and the left atrium attach, and their likely origin "can be reasonably predicted from the QRS morphology".

Ventricular tachycardia

Ventricular tachycardia (VT) is "≥3 consecutive complexes originating in the ventricles at a rate >100 bpm (cycle length: <600 ms)", bpm meaning beats per minute. It is sustained when it lasts more than 30 s or needs termination within 30 s because of hemodynamic compromise, and nonsustained when it stops by itself; monomorphic when the QRS keeps one shape from beat to beat, polymorphic when the shape changes. In the simulated VT the sinus node goes on firing at its own rate. Its P waves, marked on the strip, are unrelated to the QRS complexes. This is AV dissociation, with the ventricles faster than the atria. In the ladder each sinus impulse dies in the AV junction. AV dissociation, or fusion complexes, imply VT. The simulation does not produce capture or fusion beats, in which a well-timed sinus impulse reaches the ventricles.

VT or supraventricular tachycardia with aberrancy?

A supraventricular tachycardia (SVT) conducted with bundle branch block, or with aberrant conduction at a fast rate, also has a wide QRS. When doubt exists, "it is safest to assume any wide-complex tachycardia is VT". Two stepwise algorithms ask questions in order and stop at the first yes, which means VT. Brugada and colleagues ask: 1. Is an RS complex (an R wave followed by an S wave) absent from all precordial leads? 2. Is the interval from the onset of R to the nadir of S longer than 100 ms in any precordial lead? 3. Is there AV dissociation? The cards do not apply Brugada's fourth step, the morphology criteria in V1–V2 and V6. In the 554 wide-QRS tachycardias that Brugada and colleagues studied, the four steps had a sensitivity of 0.987 and a specificity of 0.965; independent studies did not reproduce that accuracy. Vereckei and colleagues read lead aVR alone: 1. an initial R wave; 2. an initial r or q wave wider than 40 ms; 3. a notch on the descending limb at the onset of a predominantly negative QRS; 4. a ratio vi/vt of 1 or less, where vi and vt are the voltage excursions over the first and the last 40 ms of the QRS; a ratio above 1 suggests SVT. The cards apply both algorithms to the simulated complex, measuring intervals from the QRS onset that the simulation computes. A wave counts only if it peaks, or bottoms out, before the QRS ends; a deflection still growing at the end of the QRS is taken as the start of the ST segment, not as an S or an r wave. On the simulated atrial tachycardia with RBBB, Brugada's steps and the aVR algorithm disagree.

Torsade de pointes

Torsade de pointes is "polymorphic VT that occurs in the setting of a long QT interval and is characterized by a waxing and waning QRS amplitude". It often begins with a long-short sequence, with a long coupling interval to the first beat, and may come in salvos of nonsustained VT; bradycardia, including high-grade AV block, can provide the long-short sequence. The term is best kept for a QT over 500 ms with QT–U deformity: distortion of the T and U waves, such as flattened or bifid T waves, or prominent U waves fused with the T waves. The U wave is a low, slow deflection that can follow the T wave. In the simulated heart, recovery is slowed as if by a drug that blocks the rapid delayed-rectifier potassium current (IKr), with the same change as in chapter 23: every ventricular action potential lengthens and its final phase slows. The model changes the shape of the action potential directly; it does not simulate the potassium channel. The sinus QT corrected for heart rate (QTc, by Fridericia's formula) comes out over 500 ms and the T wave lower than normal, but because every cell is changed alike, the T wave is not notched and no U wave follows it. The simulation therefore shows no QT–U deformity. A PVC is followed by its pause, the beat after the pause has a longer QT still, and a beat on its T wave starts the run. The simulation makes the QRS axis turn by moving the run's origin around the apex from beat to beat; it does not model why the axis turns in patients.

Ventricular fibrillation

Ventricular fibrillation (VF) is "rapid, grossly irregular electrical activity with marked variability in electrocardiographic waveform, ventricular rate usually >300 bpm (cycle length: <200 ms)". There are no QRS complexes to measure. The heart model has no fibrillating wavefronts. The VF on this page is phenomenological, a randomly wandering ventricular vector run fast enough to match that description, and it does not model how fibrillation works.
keypoints: A ventricular beat spreads from its origin through muscle: the QRS is wide and points away from where the beat started.

The inferior leads tell a high origin (positive: the outflow tracts) from a low one (negative: the apex or inferior wall); V1 tells the right ventricle (mainly negative) from the left ventricular lateral wall (mainly positive). Outflow-tract foci can show either pattern in V1; with an LBBB pattern, a precordial transition by V3 suggests the left side.
VT is three or more consecutive ventricular complexes faster than 100 per minute; AV dissociation or fusion complexes imply VT, and a wide-complex tachycardia in doubt is safest assumed to be VT.
Torsade de pointes is polymorphic VT with a long QT and a waxing and waning QRS amplitude, often started by a long-short sequence.
VF is rapid, grossly irregular activity, usually faster than 300 per minute, with no QRS complexes.
