chapters.title: AV block
chapters.subtitle: Conduction from atria to ventricles
chapters.lede: In the normal heart every impulse from the atria must cross the atrioventricular (AV) node and the His bundle to reach the ventricles. AV block is a delay or a failure of that crossing, and it is named by the pattern of conducted and non-conducted P waves.
chapters.body:
The AV junction and the ladder diagram

In the normal heart every impulse from the atria reaches the ventricles through the AV node and the His bundle, and block can lie in the node, within the His bundle, or below it. Neither structure produces a deflection at the body surface, so the electrocardiogram (ECG) shows only the result: how long each conducted P wave takes to reach its QRS (the PR interval), and which P waves are followed by no QRS at all. The ladder diagram under the strip shows the conduction through the AV node and His bundle that the ECG does not record. Its middle tier is the AV junction, split at the dashed line: the AV node above, the His bundle and bundle branches below. Each line is one impulse, drawn from times the simulation computed; a line that ends in a short bar is an impulse that was blocked, and the numbers are PR intervals in milliseconds. The simulated P wave is smaller than in most people: about 0.046 mV above baseline in lead II, against 0.070 mV for the median of the real normal ECGs it was fitted to. The letters above the strip mark each P wave.

First-degree AV block

First-degree AV block is "P waves associated with 1:1 atrioventricular conduction and a PR interval >200 ms". The guideline calls the term a misnomer: no P wave is blocked, each is conducted late. In the simulation the extra time is spent in the AV node, so the upper part of each AV line is longer.

Second degree: Mobitz I and Mobitz II

Second-degree AV block is "P waves with a constant rate (<100 bpm) where atrioventricular conduction is present but not 1:1". In Mobitz I (Wenckebach) a periodic single P wave is not conducted and the P waves before and after it have "inconstant PR intervals"; in Mobitz II the PR intervals are constant. In the simulated Mobitz I the AV node takes longer with each beat, by smaller and smaller steps, until one impulse fails; after the pause the PR is short again and the cycle repeats. In the simulated Mobitz II every conducted P wave has the same PR, and the block lies below the His bundle. Mobitz I is usually associated with a narrow QRS and Mobitz II most often with a wide one, though Mobitz I with a narrow QRS can arise below the node. The toggle adds right bundle branch block to every beat that crosses the His bundle: the conducted beats and, in complete block, a junctional escape.

2:1 block

In 2:1 AV block "every other P wave conducts to the ventricles". It cannot be classed as Mobitz I or Mobitz II from the strip. Both definitions turn on the PR intervals of the P waves before and after a non-conducted one: changing in Mobitz I, constant in Mobitz II. In 2:1 block each conducted P wave stands between two blocked ones, so it is always the first beat of its cycle. There is never a second conducted PR to show whether conduction was slowing before the block, and the PR is the same before and after every blocked P whatever the mechanism. The guideline's definition of Mobitz II explicitly excludes 2:1 block. If you move the block between the AV node and the His–Purkinje system, only the ladder changes. In patients the strip can still hint at the level. The guideline notes that "severe first-degree atrioventricular block (PR >0.30 s) and a narrow QRS usually indicates atrioventricular node delay", and that 2:1 block with bundle branch block "is frequently assumed to be indicative of infranodal block; however, 15% to 20% of these patients can have block in the atrioventricular node". Ambulatory monitoring or an exercise test can help: exercise improves conduction through the AV node, whereas block below the node will not resolve and is likely to worsen as the sinus rate rises.

High-grade and complete block

High-grade AV block is "≥2 consecutive P waves at a constant physiologic rate that do not conduct to the ventricles with evidence for some atrioventricular conduction"; complete (third-degree) block is "no evidence of atrioventricular conduction". In complete block the ventricles are driven by an escape rhythm. Block at the level of the AV node is associated with "a faster and more reliable" junctional escape; block within or below the His bundle with "a slower and more unpredictable" ventricular escape. A junctional escape reaches the ventricles through the His–Purkinje system, so its QRS is as narrow as a conducted one; a ventricular escape starts in muscle and is wide. The escape rates in the simulation are illustrative settings, not published values, and the simulation adds an escape rhythm only in complete block. In the simulated high-grade and 2:1 block the ventricles wait for the next conducted P wave, even through pauses longer than the interval at which the junctional escape fires in complete block. In complete block the P waves march through at their own rate, unrelated to the QRS complexes.
keypoints: First-degree AV block is 1:1 conduction with a PR over 200 ms; no P wave is blocked.
Mobitz I: a periodic single non-conducted P wave with inconstant PR intervals around it. Mobitz II: the same with constant PR intervals.
2:1 block cannot be called Mobitz I or II from the strip: there is never a second conducted PR to compare, and the guideline excludes it from Mobitz II.
High-grade block is two or more consecutive non-conducted P waves with some conduction; in complete block there is none, and an escape rhythm drives the ventricles.
Block in the AV node usually has a faster, more reliable junctional escape with a narrow QRS; block below it a slower, less predictable ventricular escape.

chapters.title: Bundle branch block
chapters.subtitle: Intraventricular conduction
chapters.lede: When a bundle branch is blocked, its territory is activated late and slowly through working muscle. The QRS widens, and its terminal forces point toward the territory activated last.
chapters.body:
How a block widens the QRS

Below the His bundle the conduction system divides. The right bundle runs to the right ventricle; the left bundle fans into an anterior fascicle, a posterior fascicle and septal fibres. In the normal heart the His–Purkinje system delivers the impulse to the endocardium of both ventricles almost at once, and the ventricles are activated within about 80 ms. When a bundle branch is blocked, its ventricle is reached instead by the wave that crosses the septum through working muscle, which conducts several times more slowly than Purkinje fibres. The blocked ventricle is activated late and alone, so its forces are no longer cancelled by the other ventricle's and form the broad terminal part of the QRS.

Right bundle branch block

The septum and the left ventricle are activated normally, so the first half of the QRS resembles the normal complex. The right ventricular free wall is activated last, rightward and anteriorly. That late force produces the R′ in V1 and the broad S in I and V6. In adults, complete right bundle branch block (RBBB) requires a QRS of 120 ms or more, an rsr′, rsR′ or rSR′ in V1 or V2, and an S wave in I and V6 longer than the R or longer than 40 ms. The same pattern with a QRS of 110 to 119 ms is incomplete RBBB; the 2009 statement prints 110 to 120 ms. The simulated RBBB axis is further right than in most patients: among the 274 real RBBB tracings whose median beat the model was fitted to, the median axis is −21.5°. In the simulated lead I the broad terminal S outweighs the small r wave, so the net area of lead I, from which the axis is computed, is negative.

Left bundle branch block

The septum is activated from right to left, the reverse of normal, so the small septal q waves of I, V5 and V6 disappear. The left ventricle is then activated slowly, from the septum around to the lateral wall. Complete left bundle branch block (LBBB) requires a QRS of 120 ms or more, a broad notched or slurred R in I, aVL, V5 and V6, no q wave in I, V5 and V6, and an R-peak time over 60 ms in V5 and V6. A QRS over 110 ms without either the RBBB or the LBBB pattern is a nonspecific intraventricular conduction delay (IVCD). Stricter criteria, proposed for the era of cardiac resynchronization therapy, require a QRS of 140 ms or more in men or 130 ms or more in women, with mid-QRS notching or slurring in at least two contiguous leads.

Hearts with LBBB are often diseased as well as blocked. In this simulation conduction everywhere, in both ventricles and the atria, is also about 16% slower, so the P wave and the PR interval lengthen too. That factor best fitted the median beat of 291 real LBBB tracings from the PTB-XL and PTB-XL+ datasets, but the fit is loose: the simulated QRS is 176 ms, against the median's 156 ms. The simulated LBBB also keeps a small q wave in V6, which the criteria exclude, and ends with a small r′ in V1, so the page reads it as a nonspecific IVCD. In the median of the real tracings, V6 has no q wave.

Fascicular block

A fascicle's territory is small and the rest of the left ventricle reaches it quickly, so a fascicular block shifts the axis without widening the QRS beyond 120 ms. In left anterior fascicular block (LAFB) the anterosuperior wall activates last, pulling the axis to between −45° and −90°, with qR in aVL, an R-peak time in aVL of 45 ms or more, and rS in II, III and aVF. Left posterior fascicular block (LPFB) moves the axis to between +90° and 180°, with rS in I and aVL and qR in III and aVF. Both fascicular blocks also require a QRS under 120 ms. When RBBB occurs with a fascicular block, the 2009 recommendations advise naming each defect (RBBB with LAFB) rather than calling it bifascicular block; beside RBBB, which already widens the QRS, this page reads the fascicular criteria without the 120 ms limit. The simulated left posterior fascicular block moves the axis only to about +75°, short of the criteria, so the page reads it as normal conduction. Neither fascicular block was used to fit the model.

Secondary ST–T changes

Repolarization follows the order of activation. When activation is abnormal, the ST segment and T wave are discordant, pointing away from the terminal QRS forces. In bundle branch block this discordance is expected and is not, by itself, a sign of ischemia.
keypoints: When a branch is blocked, its territory activates late through working muscle, and the QRS widens to 120 ms or more.
The terminal QRS points toward the territory that activated last: rightward and anterior in RBBB (R′ in V1, broad S in I and V6), leftward and posterior in LBBB (broad R in I and V6, QS or rS in V1).
LBBB removes the septal q waves of I, V5 and V6, because the septum activates from right to left.
Fascicular blocks shift the axis without widening the QRS: LAFB to between −45° and −90°, LPFB to between +90° and 180°.
In bundle branch block, discordant ST–T changes are the expected secondary pattern.

chapters.title: Pre-excitation
chapters.subtitle: Accessory pathways and the delta wave
chapters.lede: An accessory pathway connects atrium to ventricle outside the atrioventricular (AV) node. It starts ventricular activation early, from a single site, so the PR is short, the QRS begins with a slurred delta wave, and the complex points away from the pathway.
chapters.body:
Two routes to the ventricles

An accessory pathway connects an atrium to a ventricle across the AV groove, bypassing the AV node and the His–Purkinje system. It is manifest when it conducts from atrium to ventricle and so shows on the electrocardiogram (ECG), and concealed when it conducts only backward and does not change the ECG in sinus rhythm. In a manifest pathway, ventricular activation over the pathway "competes with the anterograde conduction over the AV node and spreads from the accessory pathway insertion point in the ventricular myocardium"; depending on the relative contribution of the two routes, a variable degree of pre-excitation is seen, with a short PR and slurring of the initial upstroke of the QRS, the delta wave. In the simulation the pathway's ventricular end fires 10 ms after the atrial wave reaches its atrial end. From there the wave crosses working muscle slowly, producing the delta wave; when the impulse through the AV node arrives, the Purkinje network activates the rest of the ventricles quickly, and the QRS is a fusion of the two. Slowing the AV node lets the pathway work alone for longer. The PR stays the same, but the delta wave and the QRS lengthen, until the QRS is as wide as a beat activated over the pathway alone. With the left posteroseptal pathway the QRS is that wide already.

The ECG criteria

In adults, full pre-excitation is suggested by a PR under 120 ms, assuming no block within the atria; a delta wave "which either interrupts the P wave or arises immediately after its termination"; a QRS over 120 ms; and secondary ST–T changes. How short the PR is depends on how soon the sinus impulse reaches the pathway. In the simulated heart it reaches the right anteroseptal pathway first and the left lateral one last; with a left lateral pathway the PR stays above 120 ms and the QRS below 120 ms, because the AV node's impulse arrives soon after the pathway's. The beat is pre-excited but does not meet the criteria. Left lateral pathways in particular may show varying degrees of pre-excitation because of fusion with conduction through the AV node.

Locating the pathway

The pre-excited part of the QRS starts at the pathway's ventricular end and travels away from it. In the simulated heart a left lateral or left posterior pathway activates the left ventricle first, the wave travels rightward and forward, and the QRS is mainly positive in V1. A right-sided pathway activates the right ventricle first and the left posteroseptal one the septum, and with both V1 is mainly negative. With the two posteroseptal pathways the QRS is mainly negative in III and aVF. Published algorithms read the delta wave. Arruda and colleagues used the first 20 ms of the delta wave in I, II, aVF and V1, scored positive, negative or isoelectric, with the ratio of R to S in III and V1, to place a pathway at one of 10 sites around the tricuspid and mitral rings or in the coronary venous system; prospectively, sensitivity was 90% and specificity 99%, and a truly negative delta wave in lead II predicted ablation within the coronary venous system; later series found that sign in only 70% of such pathways, with a specificity of 68%. The first step of Arruda's algorithm rules out a left free-wall pathway from the delta wave's polarity in I and V1, and in patients inferior paraseptal (posteroseptal) pathways characteristically show negative delta waves in at least two inferior leads. In a 2023 multicentre study in which the authors of EASY-WPW developed and validated their algorithm in 211 patients, Arruda's algorithm located 75% of pathways correctly, against 94% for EASY-WPW. Arruda's full decision tree is not reproduced here, and the simulated heart is not a test of it: in this idealized heart, whose ventricles are cut flat at the base, the first 20 ms of the delta wave are small, and at both posteroseptal sites they point toward the feet before the rest of the QRS turns away from them. The page therefore shows the direction of the whole pre-excited QRS, not the first 20 ms.

Pattern and syndrome

The Wolff-Parkinson-White (WPW) pattern is the ECG sign of a manifest pathway. Without documented supraventricular tachycardia (SVT) or symptoms consistent with it, the pattern is asymptomatic pre-excitation; the WPW syndrome is documented SVT, or symptoms consistent with SVT, in a patient with pre-excitation in sinus rhythm. Manifest pre-excitation is found on 0.1% to 0.3% of ECGs in the general population.

Pre-excited atrial fibrillation

In atrial fibrillation (AF) the pathway can conduct the fibrillation to the ventricles: "When AF occurs in patients with ventricular pre-excitation, if the accessory pathway has a short refractory period, this may allow for rapid pre-excited AV conduction; the resulting fast, often irregular, broad-complex tachycardia is often unstable and may lead to ventricular fibrillation." A shortest pre-excited RR interval under 250 ms during AF is one of the features associated with a higher risk of sudden cardiac death, and verapamil or diltiazem, given for a pre-excited AF, may accelerate the ventricular rate. In the simulation the fibrillatory waves are a generic signal added to the tracing, not computed from the atrial muscle. The pathway conducts at a random moment once its refractory period has passed, and after the longer pauses the AV node may join in, so each QRS is a different mixture of the two routes and its width varies from beat to beat. The slider sets the pathway's refractory period.
keypoints: Suggestive of full pre-excitation: PR under 120 ms, a delta wave, QRS over 120 ms, and secondary ST–T changes.
The pre-excited QRS is a fusion: the pathway starts it early and slowly, the AV node and His–Purkinje system finish it; slowing the node increases pre-excitation.
A pathway reached late by the sinus impulse, such as a left lateral one, may show little pre-excitation.
The pre-excited QRS points away from the pathway; published algorithms localize the pathway from the delta wave in specific leads, and the full Arruda decision tree is not reproduced here.
WPW syndrome is pre-excitation with documented SVT or symptoms consistent with SVT; pre-excited AF is fast, irregular and broad, and a shortest pre-excited RR under 250 ms marks higher risk.

chapters.title: Atrial abnormality
chapters.subtitle: The P wave and the two atria
chapters.lede: The P wave is the sum of two atria activating one after the other, the right before the left. Enlarge the left atrium and the P wave lengthens and turns negative late in V1; enlarge the right and its early, inferior forces grow.
chapters.body:
Two atria in one wave

The sinus node fires in the high right atrium. The wave spreads through the right atrium and reaches the left mainly through Bachmann’s bundle, about 30 ms after the right. The left atrium’s forces, which come later, point more to the left and back than the right atrium’s. So in lead II the P wave is one rounded hump, and in V1, which looks at the heart from the front, it is often biphasic: positive while the right atrium activates, negative while the left does.

Left atrial abnormality

Left atrial abnormality usually prolongs total atrial activation, because the left atrium begins and ends later than the right. As the delay grows, the right and left atrial peaks, normally fused, separate into a notched or double-peaked P wave. The 2009 recommendations list a P-wave duration of 120 ms or more and a widely notched P wave, with peaks 40 ms or more apart, as of equal value to the P terminal force in V1 (the product of the depth and the duration of the terminal negative part), which is the criterion used most often; a terminal P axis of −30° to −90° is also useful, and a purely negative P wave in V1 is suggestive. That document gives no cutoff for the terminal force. In a general-population study, Eranti and colleagues treated 0.04 mm·s or more as abnormal; only 0.06 mm·s or more independently predicted death and atrial fibrillation. The conduction delay often lies in Bachmann’s bundle and possibly in the left atrial muscle.

Right atrial abnormality

Right atrial abnormality raises the amplitude of the early P-wave forces and shifts the P vector to the right. A P wave taller than 2.5 mm in lead II is characteristic, often peaked, presumably because a larger right atrial component adds to the simultaneous left atrial one. An initial positive P of 1.5 mm (0.15 mV) or more in V1 or V2 also indicates right atrial abnormality; a rightward P axis and a peaked shape without increased height are supportive. Total P duration is usually normal.

The term “atrial abnormality”

Dilatation, hypertrophy of the atrial muscle, raised atrial pressure, a stiff ventricle and slow conduction inside the atria all change the P wave, often together, and the electrocardiogram (ECG) may not be able to tell them apart. The recommendations therefore prefer “left atrial abnormality” and “right atrial abnormality” to enlargement, and name intra-atrial conduction delay as its own category when the P wave widens without taller atrial components.

The simulated atria

Each control changes the simulated atria, and the P waves are computed from the new heart. Enlarging an atrium dilates its cavity. The simulated atria share one wall thickness, so thickening the walls thickens both. Slowing conduction slows the wave in the muscle of both atria and in Bachmann’s bundle. In this heart the two atria also meet along a broad septum that conducts at ordinary speed, so slowing Bachmann’s bundle alone changes little; the delay comes from the larger atrium and the slower muscle. The late left atrial activation shows as a low late shoulder in lead II rather than a separate peak, and the simulated limb-lead P waves are smaller than the median normal PTB-XL P wave the heart was fitted to, so no setting reaches the amplitude criteria, and the figure shows only the direction of each change. The measurements are made on atrial activation alone, because the atrial recovery wave starts inside the P wave. A larger or slower atrium also delays the wave's arrival at the atrioventricular node, so the PR interval lengthens with it.
keypoints: The P wave is right atrial activation followed by left; the left atrium’s later forces point more to the left and back.
Left atrial abnormality lengthens and splits the P wave: a duration of 120 ms or more, a notch of 40 ms or more, a deep, broad terminal negative P in V1.
Right atrial abnormality raises the early P forces: a P wave over 2.5 mm in II or an initial P of 1.5 mm or more in V1 or V2, with a rightward P axis.
The 2009 recommendations give no cutoff for the P terminal force in V1; 0.04 mm·s is one study’s threshold for abnormal.
The ECG may not separate dilatation, hypertrophy, pressure and slow conduction, so the recommendations prefer “atrial abnormality”.

refs.text: Eranti A, Aro AL, Kerola T, et al. Prevalence and prognostic significance of abnormal P terminal force in lead V1 of the ECG in the general population. Circ Arrhythm Electrophysiol. 2014;7(6):1116-21.

chapters.title: Ventricular hypertrophy
chapters.subtitle: Wall thickness and the voltage criteria
chapters.lede: A thicker wall takes longer to cross and produces larger forces, so the QRS grows taller and a little wider. Most hearts with hypertrophy still do not meet the voltage criteria.
chapters.body:
More muscle, larger forces

The changes that go with ventricular hypertrophy are a larger and longer QRS, a shift of its vectors, abnormal ST segments and T waves, and abnormal P waves. In this simulation the activation wave crosses the wall from the inner to the outer surface far more slowly than it runs along the inner surface, so in a thicker wall a larger area of activated muscle faces resting muscle for longer, and the left ventricle’s forces grow and last a little longer. The simulated left ventricular walls are normally 9 mm thick, within the adult range of 6 to 10 mm for men and 6 to 9 mm for women, and the right ventricular wall 4 mm, against 3 ± 1 mm. The controls thicken the walls evenly, as in concentric hypertrophy.

The voltage criteria

Amplitudes are given in millimetres at standard gain (10 mm = 1 mV). The Sokolow-Lyon index adds the S wave in V1 to the R wave in V5 or V6; over 35 mm (3.5 mV) is positive. The Cornell voltage adds the R wave in aVL to the S wave in V3: over 2.8 mV in men and 2.0 mV in women. The Cornell product multiplies the Cornell voltage by the QRS duration; over 2436 mm·ms is positive, and a later convention adds 0.8 mV to the Cornell voltage in women, as this page does, keeping the 2436 mm·ms threshold. The Peguero-Lo Presti criterion adds the deepest S wave in any lead to the S wave in V4, positive at 2.8 mV or more in men and 2.3 mV or more in women. The voltage criteria apply to adults older than 35 years.

Low sensitivity

Sensitivity is usually less than 50%, and specificity often 85% to 90%. Against autopsy in 135 patients, Sokolow-Lyon was 22% sensitive and 100% specific, Cornell voltage 42% and 96%. In another autopsy series, with specificity held at 95%, the Cornell product detected 51% of hypertrophied hearts and the Cornell voltage 36%. A systematic review of 21 studies in hypertension found a median sensitivity of 21% for Sokolow-Lyon (range 4% to 52%) with a median specificity of 89%, and concluded that the electrocardiogram (ECG) should not be used to rule hypertrophy out. Against echocardiography, Peguero-Lo Presti was 62% sensitive where Cornell voltage was 35%, with all specificities at 90% or more; in 592 older adults sensitivity and specificity were 28% and 93% for Sokolow-Lyon, 35% and 90% for Cornell voltage, and 52% and 82% for Peguero-Lo Presti. Voltage also depends on age, sex, race and build: obesity raises left ventricular mass without raising voltage, perhaps because fat insulates and moves the heart away from the electrodes. The simulated heart shows the same insensitivity: its normal Sokolow-Lyon index is well under the threshold, and the left ventricular wall has to double before the index crosses it.

Secondary ST–T abnormalities

The “typical strain” pattern of older texts consisted of J-point depression, convex, down-sloping ST depression and an asymmetrically inverted T wave. Because such changes also occur without increased work, as in dilated and hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, the 2009 recommendations call them secondary ST–T abnormalities and discourage “strain”. Their presence gives major support to a diagnosis otherwise based on voltage alone, and goes with a larger left ventricular mass and a higher risk. The toggle produces them at any wall thickness by changing recovery: the inner half of the left ventricular free wall, and nearly all of the septum, hold a slightly lower plateau and recover 20 ms earlier than the rest. That is a modelling choice that reproduces the shape, not a measured property of hypertrophied muscle.

Right ventricular hypertrophy

The right ventricle is thin, and its forces are normally hidden by the left ventricle’s. As it thickens, its rightward and anterior forces emerge: a tall R wave in V1, deep S waves in V5 and V6, and a rightward axis. The 2009 recommendations tabulate fifteen amplitude and timing criteria, among them an R wave in V1 over 6 mm, an R/S ratio in V1 over 1, an S wave in V6 over 3 mm and an R-peak time in V1 over 35 ms, with supporting signs such as an S wave in I with a Q wave in III and negative T waves in V1 to V3, and state that right axis deviation and prominent anterior forces should be required in nearly all cases. The note under the cards lists the criteria this heart meets. One row, a limb-lead index given as under 15 mm, is not computed here: as printed it would be met by most normal hearts. This heart's R wave in V1 is taller than in most adults: 0.56 mV, against 0.13 mV in the median of the real normal ECGs it was fitted to. A thicker left ventricle alone makes it taller still, so in this heart a tall R in V1 is not specific to the right ventricle.
keypoints: A thicker wall takes longer to cross and produces larger forces: taller voltages and a slightly wider QRS.
Sokolow-Lyon (SV1 + RV5 or RV6 over 3.5 mV), Cornell voltage (RaVL + SV3 over 2.8 mV in men, 2.0 mV in women), the Cornell product and Peguero-Lo Presti all measure the larger QRS.
Their sensitivity is usually under 50%, so a normal ECG does not rule hypertrophy out.
Secondary ST–T abnormalities, once called strain, support the diagnosis; the term strain is discouraged.
Right ventricular hypertrophy shows as a tall R in V1, deep S in V5 and V6 and right axis deviation, which should be present in nearly all cases.

refs.text: Tavares CAM, Samesima N, Hajjar LA, et al. Clinical applicability and diagnostic performance of electrocardiographic criteria for left ventricular hypertrophy diagnosis in older adults. Sci Rep. 2021;11(1):11516.
Molloy TJ, Okin PM, Devereux RB, et al. Electrocardiographic detection of left ventricular hypertrophy by the simple QRS voltage-duration product. J Am Coll Cardiol. 1992;20(5):1180-6.

chapters.title: ST-elevation myocardial infarction
chapters.subtitle: Acute coronary occlusion
chapters.lede: When a coronary artery closes, the muscle it supplies is injured. Current then flows between injured and healthy muscle, so the leads facing the injured wall record ST elevation and the leads on the far side record reciprocal ST depression.
chapters.body:
The injury current

The three main coronary arteries, the left anterior descending (LAD), the left circumflex (LCx) and the right coronary artery (RCA), each supply their own part of the ventricles. The bull’s-eye shows the 17 segments of the American Heart Association’s standard model of the left ventricle, coloured where the chosen artery and level supply this simulated heart. On this heart the LAD also supplies the apical lateral segment (16), which the standard model gives to the circumflex. In the simulation, muscle whose artery has closed rests at a less negative voltage, holds a lower plateau and recovers early. Current therefore flows between injured and healthy muscle both between beats and during the plateau, in opposite directions. The electrocardiogram measures the ST segment against the baseline between beats, so the two currents add: the ST segment rises in the leads that face the injured wall and falls in the leads that face it from the opposite side, the reciprocal depression.

The criteria

The Fourth Universal Definition of Myocardial Infarction asks for new ST elevation at the J point in two contiguous leads of 1 mm (0.1 mV) or more in every lead except V2 and V3, where the cut-points are 2 mm in men aged 40 or older, 2.5 mm in men under 40 and 1.5 mm in women of any age. Elevation of 1 to 2 mm confined to V2 and V3 in men, or under 1.5 mm in women, may be a normal finding. The J point is measured against the onset of the QRS, and the criteria assume no left ventricular hypertrophy and no bundle branch block. On this page, contiguous means neighbours across the chest, or two leads of one limb group (I and aVL; II, III and aVF), the groupings the definition uses for Q waves. New horizontal or downsloping ST depression of 0.5 mm or more in two contiguous leads is the corresponding sign of ischemia without elevation. The 2023 European Society of Cardiology (ESC) guideline uses the same cut-points and asks that the tracing be read within 10 minutes of first medical contact.

Finding the artery

The leads with the most elevation face the injured wall, and published rules refine the guess. In inferior ST-elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI), elevation greater in III than in II, with more depression in aVL than in I, points to the RCA; elevation in aVL, V5 or V6 with a level or raised ST segment in I points to the LCx, with a sensitivity of 83% and a specificity of 96%. The ratio of the depression in V3 to the elevation in III separates a proximal RCA occlusion (under 0.5) from a distal one (0.5 to 1.2) and from the LCx (over 1.2), with sensitivities of 84 to 91% and specificities of 91 to 95%. In anterior STEMI, elevation in aVR, complete right bundle branch block, depression in V5, elevation in V1 over 2.5 mm or inferior depression of 1 mm or more predicted an LAD occlusion before its first septal branch; a Q wave in aVL was associated with an occlusion before the first diagonal branch, and depression in aVL suggested one after it; Q waves in V4 to V6 were associated with an occlusion beyond the first septal branch.

The note under the cards applies these rules to the simulated tracing. Where a rule names a sign without a cut-point, the page counts elevation from 1 mm and depression from 0.5 mm. The rules were derived from tracings recorded on admission or before reperfusion, so the note applies them only from the hyperacute T waves to the full injury current. Later, as the ST segment falls, they mislead: at the Q-wave stage of the distal RCA occlusion, the ratio of the depression in V3 to the elevation in III is 0.31, the range of a proximal occlusion. On this heart the circumflex occlusion only just meets the criteria, in V5 and V6; its largest change is ST depression in V1 to V3, the subject of the next chapter.

The evolution

Prominent, symmetrical T waves in two or more contiguous leads, hyperacute T waves, may come before the ST segment rises. New Q waves mark necrosis, which begins minutes to hours after the insult. The definition counts as pathological any Q wave over 20 ms, or a QS complex, in V2 or V3; and in I, II, aVL, aVF or V4 to V6, a Q wave of 30 ms or more and 1 mm or more deep, or a QS complex, in two leads of one group (I and aVL; V1 to V6; II, III and aVF). Reperfusion is usually associated with a large and prompt fall in ST elevation. A consensus on Takotsubo syndrome notes that, as in acute coronary syndromes, resolution of the ST elevation is typically followed by progressive T-wave inversion.

The time slider plays an occlusion that is never reopened, as a series of changes in the territory’s muscle: early recovery for the hyperacute T wave; the injury current; necrosis that spreads from the inner wall outward, to six tenths of the wall’s thickness; late recovery of the surviving outer wall, which turns the T wave over; and finally normal recovery, which leaves the Q waves. The order follows the published descriptions, but the timing is schematic, so the slider has no time scale. Necrosis in the simulation spares the one-cell layer that stands in for the Purkinje network, a modelling choice that keeps the scar from widening the QRS on this heart.

Colours in the figure

The bull’s-eye and the two cuts colour the muscle as injured (rose), dead (taupe) or recovering late (blue); RV marks the right ventricle. The bar chart gives each lead’s ST deviation at the J point, with its cut-point as a dashed line. Leads that meet the criteria with a contiguous partner are drawn in rose, on the chart and on the tracing; a lead over its cut-point without a partner is mauve, and a lead depressed by 0.5 mm or more is blue.
keypoints: ST elevation comes from the injury current: injured and healthy muscle sit at different voltages between beats and during the plateau, and the leads facing the injury record the difference.
STEMI requires new J-point elevation in two contiguous leads: 1 mm, except in V2 and V3 (2 mm in men 40 or older, 2.5 mm in men under 40, 1.5 mm in women).
Reciprocal depression appears in the leads facing away from the injured wall: the inferior leads in a proximal LAD occlusion, aVL and I in an inferior one.
In inferior STEMI, elevation greater in III than II with more depression in aVL than I points to the RCA; the V3/III ratio separates proximal from distal RCA and from the LCx.
An infarct evolves: hyperacute T waves, ST elevation, Q waves as necrosis spreads, then T-wave inversion; the Q waves remain.

refs.text: Cerqueira MD, Weissman NJ, Dilsizian V, et al. Standardized myocardial segmentation and nomenclature for tomographic imaging of the heart. A statement for healthcare professionals from the Cardiac Imaging Committee of the Council on Clinical Cardiology of the American Heart Association. Circulation. 2002;105(4):539-42.

chapters.title: Occlusion beyond the STEMI criteria
chapters.subtitle: Occlusion without the textbook elevation
chapters.lede: Some acute occlusions and critical narrowings of a coronary artery do not meet the ST-elevation cut-points. The injured wall may face no standard lead, a narrowed artery may show its pattern only after the pain has passed, and a bundle branch block hides the injury current inside its secondary ST changes.
chapters.body:
Occlusion without ST elevation

The 2023 European Society of Cardiology (ESC) guideline on acute coronary syndromes speaks of “ongoing coronary artery acute occlusion” and of “ST-segment elevation equivalents”, and it notes that some patients “warrant … immediate reperfusion therapy despite the absence of ST-segment elevation”. It recommends the right-sided leads V3R and V4R and the posterior leads V7 to V9 in inferior ST-elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI), or when an occlusion is suspected and the standard leads are inconclusive. Posterior infarction, right ventricular infarction, the Wellens pattern and left bundle branch block are simulated on this heart; the de Winter pattern is only described. The simulation has the twelve standard leads only: V3R, V4R and V7 to V9 are not computed.

Posterior infarction

In the simulated heart the occluded territory is the basal and mid inferior and inferolateral wall (segments 4, 5, 10 and 11 of the 17-segment model), at the back and underside of the left ventricle: the wall the Fourth Universal Definition calls inferobasal, previously termed posterior. It faces away from V1 to V3, and on this heart the inferior leads see it only obliquely. Its injury current therefore shows as ST depression in V1 to V3. ST depression in V1 to V3, especially with a positive terminal T wave, suggests inferobasal ischemia, often from an occlusion of the left circumflex artery (LCx), a sign that is not specific. Leads V7 to V9, placed in the fifth intercostal space on the back, see the same injury as elevation, with a recommended cut-point of 0.5 mm, or 1 mm in men under 40. In the simulation an injury of the inferolateral wall depresses the ST segment in V1 to V3 by up to 2.2 mm and raises it in the inferior leads by less than 1 mm, so the STEMI criteria are not met. The lower panel turns V1 to V3 upside down, which shows the depression as the elevation that would be seen from the other side of the heart; this is a reading aid and does not replace posterior leads.

Right ventricular infarction

An occlusion of the right coronary artery (RCA) before its right ventricular branches injures the right ventricle (RV) as well as the inferior wall. In the right-sided leads V3R and V4R, ST elevation of 0.5 mm or more (1 mm or more in men under 30) points to right ventricular infarction, and it may be transient. ST elevation of 1 mm or more in V4R had a sensitivity of 93% and an accuracy of 93%, and it disappeared within 10 hours in half of the patients. On this heart a proximal RCA occlusion, which includes the right ventricle, raises the ST segment in V1, the lead nearest the right ventricle, by 2.1 mm, against 1.2 mm when the occlusion is beyond the right ventricular branches.

The Wellens pattern

In 1982 de Zwaan and colleagues described characteristic precordial ST–T changes in 26 of 145 patients (18%) admitted with unstable angina; 12 of the 16 who did not have surgery (75%) developed an anterior infarction, usually extensive, within a few weeks; the authors called the stenosis behind the pattern critical. In a later series the pattern was found in 180 of 1260 patients. All had a narrowing of 50% or more in the proximal left anterior descending artery (LAD), and in 33 the artery was completely occluded. The T waves in V2 and V3 are biphasic, or symmetrical and deeply inverted, after the pain has resolved, and the change may extend to V4 to V6; the ESC describes “biphasic T waves or prominent negative T waves”, and the Fourth Universal Definition “symmetrical, often deep (>2 mm), T wave inversions in the anterior precordial leads”. The mechanism is not settled; reperfusion injury and stunned myocardium are among those proposed. The simulation assumes the reperfused anterior wall recovers late, most at the epicardium, with no injury current left: the T wave turns biphasic, then deeply inverted, while the ST segment stays level. On this heart the inversion is deepest in V4, runs from V3 to V6 and into I and aVL, and V2 stays upright: the simulated anterior territory projects most strongly onto V3 to V5, as its ST elevation does in the previous chapter, rather than onto V2 and V3. The same late recovery makes the T waves in III and aVF taller, up to 7.3 mm in III at the longest delay against 0.9 mm before, because the T wave turns away from the late anterior wall and toward the inferior leads. That is an effect of the model; the descriptions quoted above do not include it.

The de Winter pattern

Instead of ST elevation, some proximal LAD occlusions show upsloping ST depression of more than 1 mm at the J point in the precordial leads running into tall, symmetrical T waves, usually with ST elevation of more than 1 mm in aVR. J-point depression of 1 to 3 mm in V1 to V6 with 1 to 2 mm of elevation in aVR has been described. The pattern was present in 35 of 1890 patients (2%) undergoing primary percutaneous coronary intervention for an LAD occlusion. Its mechanism is not established. In this simulation, ST deviation arises only from currents between muscle at different voltages, and drawing upsloping J-point depression into tall T waves across all six chest leads would mean choosing a mechanism the literature has not settled. The pattern is therefore described but not simulated.

Left bundle branch block

Left bundle branch block (LBBB) already moves the ST segment away from the main QRS deflection (chapter 14), which hides an injury current. In the Global Utilization of Streptokinase and Tissue Plasminogen Activator for Occluded Coronary Arteries (GUSTO-1) trial 0.5% of patients with infarction had LBBB, and Sgarbossa and colleagues found three independent criteria: ST elevation of 1 mm or more concordant with the QRS; ST depression of 1 mm or more in V1, V2 or V3; and ST elevation of 5 mm or more discordant with the QRS. With the criteria weighted 5, 3 and 2 points, a score of 3 or more is diagnostic. Smith’s modification replaces the third criterion with discordant ST elevation of at least 1 mm that is a quarter or more of the preceding S wave (an ST/S ratio of −0.25 or less), and any one criterion suffices: sensitivity 91% against 52% for the weighted and 67% for the unweighted rule, specificity 90% against 98% and 90%; in a validation cohort, sensitivity 80% against 49% and specificity 99% against 100%. The ESC advises managing a patient with bundle branch block and suspected ongoing ischemia like one with clear ST elevation, whether or not the block is known.

The page applies both rules to the simulated beat, measuring the ST segment at the J point against the onset of the QRS and taking the larger of the R and the S (or QS) wave as the QRS deflection. The block is the one in chapter 14. On this heart an LAD injury scores 7 points and meets Smith’s ratio in V3 and V4; an RCA injury scores 5 with concordant elevation in II, III and aVF; a circumflex injury meets neither rule.
keypoints: An occlusion can be present without meeting the STEMI cut-points: the ESC 2023 guideline speaks of ongoing acute occlusion and of ST-elevation equivalents.
A posterior (inferolateral) injury shows as ST depression in V1 to V3; posterior leads V7 to V9 see it as elevation, with a 0.5 mm cut-point.
Right ventricular involvement in an RCA occlusion is sought in V3R and V4R (0.5 mm; 1 mm in men under 30).
Biphasic or deeply inverted T waves in V2 and V3 after the pain resolves (Wellens) signal a critical stenosis of the proximal LAD.
In LBBB, concordant ST elevation, ST depression in V1 to V3, or disproportionate discordant elevation (ST/S −0.25 or less) point to an acute occlusion.

refs.text: Wang F, Zhang X, Pang H, et al. Evolution of de Winter syndrome to Wellens syndrome: a case report and literature review. Front Cardiovasc Med. 2024;11:1415306.
Anghel L, Stătescu C, Sascău RA, et al. Impact of Newly Diagnosed Left Bundle Branch Block on Long-Term Outcomes in Patients with STEMI. J Clin Med. 2024;13(18).

chapters.title: Mimics of infarction
chapters.subtitle: ST elevation without an occluded artery
chapters.lede: ST elevation does not always mean an occluded artery. Inflamed pericardium, a normal variant, an old aneurysm and stress cardiomyopathy all raise the ST segment, and published measurements help tell them apart.
chapters.body:
Each mimic beside an acute occlusion

Each mimic is drawn on the left, one beat per lead with the normal beat in grey, beside a true ST-elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI) on the right, from an occlusion of the right coronary artery (RCA) or the left anterior descending artery (LAD) simulated as in chapter 18. The lower panel shows the published measurement for each mimic, computed from the simulated beats: the ST/T ratio in V6 for pericarditis and early repolarization, the T/QRS ratio in V1 to V4 for the aneurysm, and ST deviation in aVR and V1 for Takotsubo. ST deviation is measured at the J point against the onset of the QRS. On wider screens, a cut through the heart, or the bull’s-eye for early repolarization, shows the changed muscle in colour; RV marks the right ventricle.

Acute pericarditis

The 2015 European Society of Cardiology (ESC) guideline bases the diagnosis of acute pericarditis on at least two of four findings: pericarditic chest pain, a pericardial rub, “new widespread ST-elevation or PR depression” on the electrocardiogram, and a new or worsening pericardial effusion. By its count the electrocardiogram changes in up to 60% of cases, and their evolution is “highly variable”. As summarized by Sheth and colleagues, Spodick’s four stages are: stage 1, “diffuse ST segment elevations that are concave up in all leads except V1 and aVR, with down-sloping PR segment depression”, most marked in II, aVF and V4 to V6; stage 2, “ST and PR segments normalize and T waves flatten”; stage 3, “diffuse T wave inversion”; and stage 4, T waves back to baseline. One review places stage 1 in the first two weeks, stage 2 at one to three weeks, stage 3 from the third week and stage 4 from several weeks on. In a series of 50 patients the stages came faster: stage 2 at about 1.5 days, stage 3 at about 9 days and stage 4 at 10 to 11 days.

Ginzton and Laks compared 19 patients with pericarditis and 20 with the normal variant, early repolarization. An ST/T ratio in V6, the height of the ST segment at its onset divided by the height of the T wave, of 0.25 or more identified every patient with pericarditis (positive and negative predictive values 1.0); a T wave in V6 of 0.3 mV or less had a positive predictive value of 0.85; and where V6 cannot be used, a ratio of 0.24 or more in V5, V4 or I is suggestive.

In the simulation, stage 1 injures the outer third of every ventricular wall. Because the injury surrounds the heart, most of its current cancels; what is left points toward the apex, which the open base does not balance, so the ST segment rises in most leads and falls in aVR. The atria are left uninjured, so the PR depression of stage 1 is described but not drawn: in this model an injured outer atrial wall erases the P wave instead of depressing the PR segment. Stages 2 to 4 are the same outer wall recovering a little late, then later, then normally. The pericarditis model is phenomenological and scaled by eye, and the depth of the stage 3 T-wave inversion (9.3 mm in V3) is not calibrated against patients.

Early repolarization

The early repolarization pattern is J-point elevation: the peak of a notch at the end of the QRS, or the onset of a slur, of 0.1 mV or more; ST elevation is not required. It must appear in two or more contiguous leads other than V1 to V3, with a QRS shorter than 120 ms. The ESC defines the pattern as J-point elevation of 1 mm or more in two adjacent inferior or lateral leads; the syndrome is that pattern in a person resuscitated from otherwise unexplained ventricular fibrillation or polymorphic ventricular tachycardia. On this heart, the outer quarter of the inferior wall and the apex loses part of its plateau just after the upstroke, as though the notch of its action potential were held, and recovers a little early. The result is a notch or slur at the end of the QRS, J-point elevation of 1.3 to 1.8 mm in II, III and aVF and of 1.1 to 2.2 mm in V4 to V6, and tall T waves; the ST/T ratio in V6 is 0.24, just on the normal-variant side of Ginzton’s cut-point. No lead but aVR is depressed by 0.5 mm or more. The region is a modelling choice: placed on the inferior and inferolateral walls, the same change also produced ST depression of up to 1.4 mm in V1 to V3 and aVL, the reciprocal picture of an inferior infarction. In a patient, reciprocal depression helps to separate an infarction from early repolarization and pericarditis.

Left ventricular aneurysm

A previous infarction may leave persistent ST elevation, the “left ventricular aneurysm” morphology, which mimics an acute one. In comparison with acute anterior infarction from a proven LAD occlusion, the best discriminator was the sum of the T-wave amplitudes in V1 to V4 divided by the sum of the QRS amplitudes there: a ratio over 0.22 favoured acute infarction and 0.22 or less an aneurysm, misclassifying 4 of 59 tracings (6.8%). In a validation of 59 acute infarctions and 16 aneurysms the same rule had a sensitivity of 91.5% and a specificity of 68.8% for acute infarction; a T/QRS ratio of 0.36 or more in any one of V1 to V4 had the same sensitivity and a specificity of 81.3%. In the simulated aneurysm, the mid-LAD territory of the left ventricle is scar through the full thickness of the wall, and a rim of living muscle two cells wide keeps a mild injury and recovers late; how late is a free choice in this model, made to keep the T waves small. The tracing has Q waves in V3 to V6 and ST elevation that meets the STEMI cut-points, but its T/QRS ratio is 0.20, against 0.61 for the acute occlusion of the same artery beside it. The QRS amplitude is taken as the larger of the R wave and the Q or S wave in each lead.

Takotsubo syndrome

The International Takotsubo (InterTAK) criteria count new electrocardiographic abnormalities, ST elevation, ST depression, T-wave inversion and prolongation of the corrected QT interval (QTc), “however, rare cases exist without any ECG changes”. In the InterTAK registry ST elevation was present in 44% of patients, ST depression in 8%, T-wave inversion in 41% and left bundle branch block in 5%. In one small series cited by the same consensus, of 13 patients with each condition, pathological Q waves were seen in 15% with Takotsubo against 69% with anterior STEMI. The elevation is centred on V2 to V5 and lead II, whereas in anterior STEMI it centres on V1 to V4, I and aVL, and elevation limited to the inferior leads is “distinctly uncommon”. Life-threatening ventricular arrhythmias occur in 3.0 to 8.6% of patients, mostly with a QTc over 500 ms. In Kosuge’s study of 33 patients with Takotsubo and 342 with anterior infarction, ST depression in aVR without ST elevation in V1, measured 80 ms after the J point, had a sensitivity of 91% and a specificity of 95% for Takotsubo, as tabulated by Frangieh and colleagues. In their own admission tracings with ST elevation, from 111 patients with Takotsubo and 106 with STEMI and measured at the J point, the same sign had a sensitivity of 38% and a specificity of 95%.

The simulated acute phase is an injury of the apical left ventricle in every wall, beyond the territory of any one artery; the later phase is the same apex recovering late. On this heart the acute tracing has ST elevation from V2 to V6 and in I, II and aVF, depression in aVR and none in V1, while the proximal LAD occlusion beside it raises I, aVL and V2 to V6 and lowers the inferior leads. The later phase has deep, widespread T-wave inversion and a QTc of 475 ms.
keypoints: Pericarditis raises the ST segment in most leads except aVR and V1, often with PR depression; an ST/T ratio of 0.25 or more in V6 separated it from early repolarization.
Early repolarization is J-point elevation, a notch or slur of 0.1 mV or more, in two contiguous inferior or lateral leads.
Persistent ST elevation after an old anterior infarct comes with small T waves: a T/QRS ratio in V1 to V4 of 0.22 or less favours aneurysm over acute infarction.
Takotsubo injures the apex beyond any one artery: ST elevation centred on V2 to V5 and II, with depression in aVR and no elevation in V1.
On the simulated heart, pericarditis, early repolarization and the aneurysm all meet the STEMI cut-points: the cut-points alone do not separate them.

chapters.title: Potassium
chapters.subtitle: Hyperkalemia and hypokalemia
chapters.lede: Potassium sets how quickly the ventricles recover and, at high levels, how quickly the heart conducts. Raise it and the T wave narrows and peaks before conduction slows; lower it and the T wave flattens as a U wave appears.
chapters.body:
What the slider changes

The slider sets the serum potassium of the simulated heart. Potassium acts on the cells' action potentials and conduction, and the tracing is computed from the cells. The model has no ion channels, so the link from potassium to the action potential is phenomenological, chosen to reproduce the published electrocardiogram (ECG) descriptions. Between 3.5 and 5.0 mmol/L the simulation leaves the heart unchanged. Above 5.0 mmol/L ventricular recovery becomes shorter and steeper; above 6.0 the P wave shrinks; above 6.5 conduction slows in the atria and the ventricles. Below 3.5 mmol/L the final phase of repolarization slows, the plateau of the inner wall declines faster than that of the outer wall, and a small late wave, the simulation's stand-in for the U wave, follows the T wave. The lower right panel shows the action potential of a ventricular muscle cell, with the normal one in grey. The model holds the resting potential at −85 mV at every level. In reality it rises by about 18 mV as potassium doubles from 4 to 8 mmol/L, and falls in hypokalemia; advanced hypokalemia also brings a taller, wider P wave, a slightly longer PR interval and a wider QRS. None of these changes is simulated.

Hyperkalemia

The sequence usually taught as potassium rises is "peaked T waves, PR interval prolongation, QRS prolongation, loss of P wave, escape rhythms, 'sine wave' configuration, ventricular fibrillation, and pulseless activity or asystole". A raised extracellular potassium shortens the action potential, and ventricular repolarization becomes more synchronous: the T wave narrows and peaks. It also depolarizes the resting membrane, which first speeds and then, above about 8 mmol/L in experimental models, slows conduction: the P wave broadens and disappears and the QRS widens. In patients it is not uncommon for the P wave to disappear and the QRS to widen at 7 to 8 mmol/L, and the sinus impulse can still reach the ventricles after the P wave has gone (sinoventricular conduction), as it does in the simulated heart. At the top of the slider the QRS runs into the T wave, the pattern El-Sherif shows at a potassium of 10 mmol/L. The simulation stops there: it does not produce the sine wave, escape rhythms or ventricular arrhythmias.

Bands and severity grades

The bands under the slider are named for the pattern the simulated ECG shows in each, because published grades of severity disagree. The two upper bands use the cut-points of El-Sherif's table, which lists tall, peaked, narrow-based T waves and fascicular blocks from 5.5 to 7.5 mmol/L; first-degree atrioventricular (AV) block, a smaller and then absent P wave, sinus arrest and ST depression from 7.5 to 10.0; and, beyond the slider, atypical bundle branch block, ventricular tachycardia and fibrillation above 10.0. El-Sherif's table calls 5.5 to 7.5 mmol/L mild and 7.5 to 10.0 moderate hyperkalemia. Weiss calls 5.5 to 6.0 mmol/L mild, 6.0 to 7.0 moderate and anything above 7.0 severe, and Durfey studied 6.5 mmol/L or more as severe hyperkalemia. Weiss puts conduction slowing above about 8 mmol/L in animal models, though in patients the P wave can disappear and the QRS widen at 7 to 8 mmol/L. The same review warns that heart block, asystole and ventricular tachycardia or fibrillation can occur above 7.0, and stresses that the level at which any change appears varies considerably between people. The lowest band marks the levels at which the simulated late wave stands taller than the T wave in at least one lead: 2.7 mmol/L and below.

The ECG follows the serum level loosely. Among 90 patients with potassium of 6.0 mmol/L or more, about half (52%) had a new or resolving peaked or symmetric T wave; peaked T waves were seen in 32% on study review but reported in 3% of official readings, and no T-wave amplitude could be set as a diagnostic threshold. The authors judged the ECG insensitive. The simulated heart shows the changes every time, in the same order.

Which changes predict harm

Among 188 patients with potassium of 6.5 mmol/L or more, 15% had an adverse event within six hours, and every one of them had at least one hyperkalemic ECG abnormality beforehand. QRS prolongation beyond 110 ms (relative risk 4.74), a heart rate below 50 per minute (relative risk 12.29) and a junctional rhythm (relative risk 7.46) marked higher risk; peaked T waves did not (relative risk 0.77, not significant). Most adverse events were symptomatic bradycardia (22 of the 28 patients with an event), so the slow heart rate partly overlaps the outcome it predicts. The QRS card is flagged once the QRS passes 110 ms.

Hypokalemia

Low potassium slows the final phase of repolarization, giving the action potential a long tail; it prolongs the plateau of the Purkinje fibres but shortens that of the ventricular muscle, so the conducting system recovers later than the muscle around it. El-Sherif lists "decreased amplitude and broadening of the T waves; prominent U waves; ST segment depression; and T and U wave fusion, which is seen in severe hypokalemia", and states that when the U wave exceeds the T wave in amplitude, potassium is below 3 mmol/L. The American Heart Association (AHA) statement on repolarization puts the threshold at 2.7 mmol/L and adds that the apparent growth of the U wave may be its fusion with the T wave rather than a larger U wave. The U wave is most evident in V2 and V3, and at heart rates of 50 to 100 per minute its peak usually falls more than 150 ms after the T-wave peak. Hypokalemia is also a risk factor for torsade de pointes.

The same AHA statement describes the U wave as a mechanoelectric phenomenon, which a model of electrical recovery cannot produce. The simulated late wave is a stand-in: a small voltage in the fast-conducting subendocardial layer some 170 to 290 ms after that layer recovers, sized so that the published sequence appears in order. Its timing and size are schematic.
keypoints: Rising potassium first narrows and peaks the T wave, then slows conduction: a longer PR, a smaller and then absent P wave, a wider QRS, until the QRS runs into the T wave.

The ECG is an insensitive guide to the serum level: only about half of patients with potassium of 6.0 mmol/L or more had a new or resolving peaked or symmetric T wave<cite data-ref="montague2008"></cite>.
In hyperkalemia, a QRS beyond 110 ms, a heart rate below 50 and a junctional rhythm marked higher short-term risk; peaked T waves did not<cite data-ref="durfey2017"></cite>.

Hypokalemia lowers and broadens the T wave, depresses the ST segment and brings out the U wave; a U wave taller than the T wave suggests potassium below 3 mmol/L (2.7 in the AHA statement)<cite data-ref="elsherif2011,rautaharju2009"></cite>.
Published severity grades disagree, and the potassium level at which each change appears varies widely between patients; in the simulation it is fixed.

chapters.title: Calcium and temperature
chapters.subtitle: The plateau, and the J wave of hypothermia
chapters.lede: Calcium sets how long the ventricular plateau lasts, so its classic effect is to move the T wave later or earlier without reshaping it. Cold lengthens every interval and notches the outer wall’s action potential, which produces the J (Osborn) wave.
chapters.body:
Calcium and the plateau

Low extracellular calcium prolongs phase 2, the plateau of the ventricular action potential, and high calcium shortens it. On the electrocardiogram (ECG), in El-Sherif’s words, hypocalcemia "results in prolonged ST segment and QT interval while hypercalcemia ... results in shortening of both intervals"; in hypercalcemia the changes are "limited to shortening or elimination of the ST segment and decreased QTc [corrected QT] interval". The ST segment is the plateau: while every cell holds it, no current flows between them. A longer plateau lengthens the ST segment, and the T wave, which marks recovery, arrives later.

The calcium slider lengthens or shortens the plateau of every ventricular cell and changes nothing else, so the ST segment and the QT change while the T wave keeps its shape. This link from calcium to the plateau is phenomenological and simplified. In patients, hypocalcemia can also alter the T wave ("upright, low, flat, or sharply inverted T waves in leads with an upright QRS complex"), and hypercalcemia, like hypothermia, has long been reported to produce J waves; neither appears in this simulation. Although hypocalcemia also prolongs the QT, it has been linked to torsade de pointes only in rare cases. No numeric QT cut-points for calcium disorders could be verified for this chapter, so none is given. The slider’s values are on the model’s scale: its action potential is unchanged at 2.4 mmol/L.

Hypothermia

Hypothermia is generally defined as a core temperature below 35 °C. Its classic ECG findings are "J (Osborn) waves, interval (PR, QRS, QT) prolongation, and atrial and ventricular dysrhythmias"; it can also produce changes that mimic acute ischemia or infarction, and blunt the expected ECG findings of hyperkalemia. The J wave is a dome or hump at the junction of the QRS and the ST segment. Experimental evidence places its origin in the ventricular wall: it is "inscribed as a consequence of a transmural voltage gradient caused by the manifestation of an AP [action potential] notch in epicardium but not endocardium", owing to an uneven distribution across the wall of the transient outward potassium current (Ito).

How the simulation builds the J wave

Below 35 °C each cell in the outer 40% of the ventricular free walls gains a notch: just after its upstroke, its voltage dips and then returns over about 50 ms, deeper as the temperature falls. The endocardium keeps its plateau, so during those milliseconds current flows across the wall, and leads facing the epicardium record a positive deflection at the end of the QRS. The action-potential shape the model uses for every cell cannot include a transient notch (lowering the whole plateau would instead produce the ST elevation of an injury current), so the notched heart is computed from two simulations: the cold heart, minus a heart in which only those epicardial cells fire a brief pulse. In the model every lead is a linear sum of the cells' voltages, so the difference is exactly the ECG of the notched heart. As the temperature falls, conduction slows in the atrioventricular (AV) node and throughout the heart, and recovery slows too, lengthening the PR, the QRS and the QT. The rates of slowing per degree, and the growth of the J wave with cold, are schematic: the published sources do not give an amplitude for each temperature, and the simulation shows the direction of each change rather than its size.
keypoints: Low calcium lengthens the plateau, and with it the ST segment and the QT; high calcium shortens or eliminates the ST segment<cite data-ref="elsherif2011"></cite>.

In the simulation only the plateau changes, so the T wave keeps its shape; in patients hypocalcemia can also alter the T wave. No numeric QT cut-point for calcium disorders could be verified for this chapter.
Hypothermia below 35 °C brings J (Osborn) waves, a longer PR, QRS and QT, and dysrhythmias; it can mimic ischemia and blunt the signs of hyperkalemia<cite data-ref="mattu2002"></cite>.
The J wave comes from a transmural voltage gradient: an action-potential notch in the epicardium that the endocardium lacks<cite data-ref="antzelevitch2016"></cite>.
The size of the simulated J wave at each temperature is schematic.

chapters.title: Drugs
chapters.subtitle: Repolarization, conduction, psychotropics
chapters.lede: Drugs change the electrocardiogram (ECG) by changing the action potential: blocking the rapid delayed-rectifier potassium current (I<sub>Kr</sub>), carried by the human ether-à-go-go-related gene (hERG) channel, lengthens the QT; blocking the sodium current widens the QRS; and digoxin sags the ST segment. The ECG changes with lithium and clozapine are less specific.
chapters.body:
Drugs in the model

Each section changes the simulated heart the way a class of drug changes the cardiac action potential. The model has no ion channels, so each drug is represented phenomenologically, as a change to the length or shape of every cell's action potential, or to the speed of conduction, chosen to reproduce published ECG findings. No slider position is the dose of any drug.

QT-prolonging drugs

The section on QT-prolonging drugs lengthens every ventricular action potential and slows its final phase, a stand-in for block of the rapid delayed-rectifier potassium current (IKr) carried by the hERG channel (named for the human ether-à-go-go-related gene, KCNH2). Because the QT shortens as the heart rate rises, it is corrected for rate: Bazett divides the QT by the square root of the RR interval in seconds, Fridericia by its cube root. Bazett overcorrects at fast rates and undercorrects at slow ones, overstating the corrected QT (QTc) particularly above 85 per minute. In this simulation only each action potential's duration scales with rate, with the cube root of the RR interval (a modelling choice); the spread of activation and the final phase of recovery do not. So the simulated QT shortens less with rate than a person's does, and even Fridericia's QTc creeps up at fast rates: in the drug-free heart it is 397 ms at 50 per minute and 440 ms at 120. In population data Fridericia's QTc instead tends to fall as the rate rises (a correlation of −0.26 to −0.32 with heart rate).

In the 2009 recommendations for interpreting the ECG, a QTc of 450 ms or more in men, or 460 ms or more in women, is prolonged. The 2010 statement on preventing torsade de pointes (TdP) in hospital instead treats a QTc above the 99th percentile, about 470 ms in men and 480 ms in women, as abnormally prolonged; above 500 ms is highly abnormal, and data from congenital long-QT syndrome tie it to a two- to threefold higher risk of TdP. After a drug with TdP risk is given, prompt action is indicated if the QTc exceeds 500 ms or has risen by at least 60 ms from the pre-drug baseline. The cards check both action thresholds against the simulated beat, using the drug-free heart at the same rate as the pre-drug baseline.

The congenital loss of IKr (long-QT type 2) gives bifid, notched T waves, and its T waves are small: 0.13 mV in lead II on average, against 0.36 and 0.37 mV in the two other genotypes Moss compared. After an overdose the ECG should be checked for QT-U distortion, a sign of impending TdP. The simulated T wave lengthens and flattens but is not notched: every ventricular cell changes in the same way, so recovery stays one wave; chapter 24 notches the T wave of long-QT type 2 by delaying the right ventricle's recovery.

The panel under the cards summarizes the evidence on psychiatric drugs. For most classes, evidence of clinically meaningful QT prolongation "remains minimal", and Beach's review advises weighing the patient's other QT risk factors when prescribing.

Sodium-channel blockers and tricyclic overdose

The sodium-channel section slows conduction through every tissue and slows each cell's upstroke, as block of the fast sodium current does: the P wave, the PR and the QRS all lengthen. In one study of 49 patients with acute tricyclic antidepressant overdose, no seizures or ventricular arrhythmias occurred when the maximal limb-lead QRS was under 100 ms; at 100 ms or more, 34% had seizures and 14% ventricular arrhythmias, and ventricular arrhythmias occurred only at 160 ms or more. In that study serum drug levels predicted neither. In another, of 79 patients, a terminal R wave in aVR of 3 mm or more had a sensitivity of 81% and a positive predictive value of 43% for seizures or arrhythmias, against 82% and 35% for a QRS over 100 ms, and it was the only independent ECG predictor (odds ratio 6.9, 95% confidence interval 1.2 to 40). Pooled across 18 studies, the QRS predicted seizures with a sensitivity and specificity of 0.69 and 0.69, and ventricular arrhythmias with 0.79 and 0.46; the serum drug concentration did about as well, and the authors judged the two to have "similar but relatively poor performance for predicting complications".

The simulation reproduces the QRS widening but not the terminal R wave in aVR. Slowing every pathway by the same factor stretches the QRS in time without turning its terminal forces rightward, so the terminal R in aVR stays small and even shrinks; the card reports the measured value. The QRS card measures from the first ventricular activation to the last, across all leads. That is at least as long as the widest limb-lead QRS that Boehnert and Lovejoy grouped patients by, so the group on the card can be higher than theirs would be, never lower. Tricyclic and tetracyclic antidepressants can also unmask a Brugada pattern, as can class IC antiarrhythmic drugs; this simulation does not show it (chapter 24 simulates the Brugada pattern).

Digoxin

Digoxin changes the ECG at therapeutic levels as well as in toxicity: "down-sloping ST segment depression ('scooped out' or 'reverse tick' appearance), flattened/inverted T waves and increased U wave amplitude" occur in both, and serum levels "do not correlate consistently with toxicity". The hallmark of toxicity is "increased automaticity coupled with concomitant conduction delay": frequent premature ventricular complexes, bradyarrhythmias, atrial tachycardia with block, junctional tachycardia and bidirectional ventricular tachycardia. The digoxin section makes the plateau of the inner half of the wall decline faster, which depresses the ST segment in leads facing the epicardium; it also shortens the action potential and slows its final phase (a lower T wave) and slows the atrioventricular (AV) node (a longer PR). The arrhythmias are not simulated. Digoxin also has "a QT-interval shortening effect": in a population cohort, people taking it had shorter QT intervals than those who did not. The simulated QT barely changes, so this shortening is not shown.

Lithium and clozapine

In a review of 56 reports, T-wave inversion was the ECG finding most often linked to lithium; sinus node dysfunction, sinoatrial block, PR and QT prolongation and ventricular tachyarrhythmias were also reported, with case reports of heart block and the Brugada pattern. The changes depended on the serum level and the duration of treatment, and there are no standardized ECG guidelines. The simulated lithium heart has a slower sinus rate and a flatter T wave, made by shrinking the spread of recovery times across the ventricles; the size of both changes is illustrative. Shrinking that spread also shortens the simulated QT slightly, the opposite of the QT prolongation reported with lithium, and correcting for the slow simulated rate lowers both QTc values further. The QTc cards therefore read low; the note under them gives the numbers.

In one series, clozapine myocarditis began between days 10 and 33 of treatment (83% between days 14 and 21), and stopping clozapine was advised if troponin exceeded twice the upper limit of normal or C-reactive protein exceeded 100 mg/L. Tachycardia was reported in 58% of published cases. In a retrospective health-record study of 254 suspected episodes in 228 patients, 29 of them confirmed as probable myocarditis, a heart rate above 90 per minute had a sensitivity of 100% for myocarditis but a specificity of 9.5%. No ECG change is specific: sinus tachycardia, arrhythmias, QT prolongation, T-wave inversion and ST-segment elevation are among those reported. The simulated clozapine heart has a faster sinus rate and no other change. The ECG can raise suspicion of myocarditis, but the monitoring protocol relies on troponin and C-reactive protein.
keypoints: Correct the QT for rate and name the formula: Bazett overstates the QTc at fast heart rates<cite data-ref="rautaharju2009,sagie1992,drew2010"></cite>.
After a drug with torsade risk, act if the QTc exceeds 500 ms or rises by 60 ms or more from baseline<cite data-ref="drew2010"></cite>.

In tricyclic overdose, one study saw no seizures or ventricular arrhythmias below a QRS of 100 ms and arrhythmias only from 160 ms; in another, a terminal R in aVR of 3 mm or more was the only independent ECG predictor. Pooled across studies, the QRS and the drug level predict complications similarly and relatively poorly<cite data-ref="boehnert1985,liebelt1995,bailey2004"></cite>.
Digoxin effect (down-sloping ST depression, flat T waves) appears with or without toxicity, and serum levels do not track toxicity reliably<cite data-ref="andrews2023"></cite>.

T-wave inversion is the ECG finding most often reported with lithium; clozapine myocarditis has no specific ECG sign, and tachycardia is sensitive but not specific<cite data-ref="mehta2017,li2025,segev2021"></cite>.
