chapters.title: Channelopathies
chapters.subtitle: Long QT, short QT, Brugada
chapters.lede: In the long and short QT syndromes the cells of a structurally normal heart repolarize too slowly or too quickly: the heart-rate-corrected QT interval (QTc) lengthens or shortens and the T wave changes shape. In Brugada syndrome the ST segment rises in V1 and V2; whether abnormal repolarization or slowed conduction in the right ventricular outflow tract, or both, causes that pattern is still debated<cite data-ref="antzelevitch2016"></cite>. Catecholaminergic polymorphic ventricular tachycardia, another inherited channelopathy, is diagnosed in a structurally normal heart with a normal resting electrocardiogram, from ventricular tachycardia brought on by exercise or emotion<cite data-ref="zeppenfeld2022"></cite>.
chapters.body:
What the simulation changes

Every cell in the simulated heart follows one action-potential shape, stretched to its own duration. The simulation represents long QT, short QT and the Brugada patterns as changes to that shape; it does not model ion currents. Long QT lengthens the action potential and changes how its last phase falls, short QT shortens it, and the Brugada patterns lower the plateau of the epicardium of the right ventricle (RV) beneath V1 and V2. The changes are phenomenological, chosen so that the surface electrocardiogram (ECG) shows the published patterns. The heart’s geometry and activation sequence are untouched, so the QRS lasts as long as before; the Brugada patterns do reshape its end in V1 and V2, adding a small terminal r′ wave.

Long QT: three genotypes and their T waves

Long QT syndrome (LQTS) types 1, 2 and 3 (LQT1 to LQT3) arise from variants in KCNQ1, KCNH2 and SCN5A, the genes behind the slow and rapid delayed-rectifier potassium currents (IKs and IKr) and the sodium current (INa). Their T waves differ: early-onset broad T waves in LQT1, bifid (notched) T waves in LQT2 and late-onset T waves in LQT3. In the families Moss studied, the interval from QRS onset to T-wave onset in lead II, corrected for rate, was 243 ms in LQT1, 290 ms in LQT2 and 341 ms in LQT3; the T wave was smallest in LQT2 (0.13 mV, against 0.37 and 0.36 mV) and longest in LQT1 (262 ms, against about 190 ms). The patterns overlap. Typical ST–T patterns were present in 88% of LQT1 and LQT2 carriers and 65% of LQT3 carriers.

In the simulation, LQT1 lengthens every action potential and slows its last phase, which spreads the T wave out. LQT3 lengthens the plateau: the ST segment grows and a normal-looking T wave arrives late. For LQT2 the RV recovers 110 ms after the left ventricle (LV), so the T wave forms in two steps, low and notched. That split reproduces the published shape; the model does not say where recovery is delayed in patients.

Making the diagnosis

The diagnostic score introduced in 1993 and updated to 2011 is printed in Schwartz, Crotti and Insolia 2012. A rate-corrected QT (QTc, by Bazett’s formula) of 480 ms or more scores 3 points, 460 to 479 ms 2, and 450 to 459 ms in a man 1. Torsade de pointes scores 2; T-wave alternans, notched T waves in three leads and a QTc of 480 ms or more at minute 4 of exercise recovery 1 each; a low heart rate for age 0.5; syncope with stress 2 or without stress 1; congenital deafness 0.5; a family member with definite LQTS 1; and unexplained sudden death before 30 in the immediate family 0.5. One point or less means a low probability, 1.5 to 3 an intermediate one. For the top band the paper’s table and text disagree: the table, as printed in the author manuscript, says 5 points or more, apparently a misprint, while the text says 3.5 points is sufficient for a high probability. The score above the cards follows the text, so every total falls in a band.

The 2022 European Society of Cardiology (ESC) guideline diagnoses LQTS with a QTc of 480 ms or more on repeated 12-lead ECGs, a score above 3, or a pathogenic mutation; with arrhythmic syncope, a QTc of 460 ms or more is enough to consider it. Its modified score gives 3.5 points both to a QTc of 480 ms or more and to a pathogenic mutation, so either alone passes the threshold.

Short QT

In adults a QTc of 390 ms or less is short. The ESC diagnoses short QT syndrome (SQTS) with a QTc of 360 ms or less plus a pathogenic mutation, a family history of SQTS, or survival from ventricular tachycardia or fibrillation (VT or VF) without heart disease, and says it should be considered with a QTc of 320 ms or less alone. In 61 reported cases the mean QTc was 306.7 ms, and symptomatic patients ranged from 248 to 381 ms. In the simulation every action potential is 80 ms shorter.

Brugada patterns

Only the coved type 1 pattern is diagnostic: ST elevation of 2 mm (0.2 mV) or more in at least one right precordial lead, V1 to V3 in the 2016 consensus, placed in the fourth, third or second intercostal space; the 2022 ESC guideline names V1 or V2. The pattern may appear spontaneously or be brought out by sodium-channel-blocking drugs or fever. A spontaneous type 1 pattern without other heart disease establishes Brugada syndrome; one that appears only on provocation also needs other clinical features, such as documented VF or polymorphic VT, arrhythmic syncope or a relevant family history. The type 2, saddle-back pattern has ST elevation of 0.5 mm or more (generally 2 mm or more in V2) followed by a positive T wave in V2, and cannot substitute for type 1. The 2012 consensus keeps only these two patterns, folding the old type 3 into the saddle-back.

The simulated pattern comes from the basal RV epicardium that faces the front of the chest, the model’s stand-in for the right ventricular outflow tract, the region most affected in Brugada syndrome. Its plateau is lowered after the spike and climbs back slowly, so during the ST segment current flows between it and the muscle beneath, most strongly at first. The two types differ only in when the region recovers. For type 1 it recovers 60 ms late: the ST segment falls from a high J point straight into a negative T wave, the coved shape. For type 2 it recovers 60 ms early: the falling ST segment reaches a trough and rises again into an upright T wave, the saddle. The timing was chosen to reproduce the two published shapes, and the model makes no claim about how they arise in patients.

Placing V1 and V2 in the third or second intercostal space increases the sensitivity of the ECG, and the pattern is sometimes concealed, recorded only in these upper leads. The simulation cannot show this: its right ventricle ends at the valve plane, with no outflow tract rising above it, and the muscle with the lowered plateau sits level with the fourth-interspace electrodes, so moving V1 and V2 up carries them away from it. The model also produces a small mirror-image ST depression in V5 and V6; the published criteria concern V1 to V3.

Early repolarization: pattern and syndrome

The early repolarization (ER) pattern is defined by Jp, the peak of a notch or the onset of a slur at the end of the QRS: a Jp of 0.1 mV or more, with or without ST elevation, in two or more contiguous leads other than V1 to V3, with a QRS under 120 ms. The ESC defines the pattern as J-point elevation of 1 mm or more in two adjacent inferior or lateral leads, and the syndrome as that pattern in a patient resuscitated from otherwise unexplained VF or polymorphic VT; in a victim of sudden death with a negative autopsy and chart review, and an ECG recorded before death that shows the pattern, it says the syndrome should be considered. The pattern was considered benign until 2008, when it was linked to cardiac arrest from idiopathic VF. Experimental work attributes the J wave to a notch early in the action potential of the epicardium but not the endocardium. This chapter does not draw the pattern; chapter 20 shows it by lowering the early plateau of the inferolateral outer wall, and chapter 22 draws the J wave of hypothermia from a transient notch, computed by superposing two simulations.
keypoints: The simulation represents long QT, short QT and Brugada as changes to the action potential’s shape and duration, chosen to reproduce the published ECGs; it does not model ion currents.
LQT1 tends to give a broad T wave, LQT2 a low, notched one and LQT3 a late one after a long ST segment; the patterns overlap.

ESC 2022 diagnoses LQTS with a QTc of 480 ms or more on repeated ECGs, a score above 3 or a pathogenic mutation. The 2012 Schwartz score’s text puts high probability at 3.5 points, though its table, apparently misprinted, says 5.
SQTS is diagnosed with a QTc of 360 ms or less plus a mutation, a family history or survived VT or VF, and considered at 320 ms or less.

Only the coved type 1 Brugada pattern, 2 mm or more in V1 or V2 (V1 to V3 in the 2016 consensus), is diagnostic: when it appears spontaneously, or, after a sodium-channel blocker or fever, only with a clinical feature such as arrhythmic syncope or documented VF.

The early repolarization pattern becomes a syndrome in a patient resuscitated from otherwise unexplained VF or polymorphic VT, and the syndrome should be considered in a sudden-death victim with a negative autopsy and an earlier ECG showing the pattern.

chapters.title: Cardiomyopathy, pericardium and pulmonary embolism
chapters.subtitle: Structural disease in one simulated heart
chapters.lede: Five conditions, each simulated in the same heart: walls that thicken, a right ventricle that scars, walls infiltrated by amyloid, fluid around the heart, and a right ventricle suddenly overloaded.
chapters.body:
Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy

In adults, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is defined by a left ventricular (LV) wall thickness of 15 mm or more that is not explained solely by abnormal loading conditions; walls of 13 to 14 mm require evaluation of other features, including family history, genetic findings and electrocardiogram (ECG) abnormalities. The ECG can also point to a cause: pre-excitation (Danon disease and PRKAG2 disease, both glycogen storage disorders, and Fabry disease), atrioventricular (AV) block (amyloidosis, sarcoidosis), low voltage (amyloidosis) or an axis between −90° and ±180°, sometimes called northwest (Noonan syndrome). Voltage criteria alone are seen in under 2% of patients, while T-wave inversion appears in 62% to over 90% of patients, depending on the cohort; inversion in V4 to V6 was found in 38% of patients with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy against 0.8% of athletes. Pathological hypertrophy commonly brings T-wave inversion in the inferior and lateral leads, ST depression and pathological Q waves, and deep T-wave inversion in V5 and V6 should prompt imaging for apical hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. In the simulation the LV wall is 18 mm. The model thickens it evenly all round, septum included, so the hypertrophy is concentric; asymmetric septal hypertrophy and the apical form are not represented. The T-wave inversion comes from making the inner half of the wall recover early, a modelling choice.

Arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy

Fibrofatty tissue replaces the muscle of the right ventricle (RV). The classic description puts early disease in the inflow, the outflow and the apex, but it predates genetic testing: in 74 mutation-positive patients the basal inferior and basal anterior walls were the most often affected, and the apex was involved only in advanced disease. The 2010 task force criteria count T-wave inversion in V1, V2 and V3 or beyond, after age 14 and without complete right bundle branch block (RBBB), as a major criterion, and inversion in V1 and V2 alone as minor. An epsilon wave, reproducible low-amplitude signals between the end of the QRS and the start of the T wave in V1 to V3, is major. A terminal activation duration of 55 ms or more, from the nadir of the S wave to the end of the QRS in V1, V2 or V3, without complete RBBB, is minor. The 2023 European Society of Cardiology (ESC) guideline urges caution with epsilon waves: they are “frequently overdiagnosed”, there is “poor agreement even between experts” on their presence, and they occur with severe structural disease, so they “add little to the diagnosis”.

In the simulation about three cells in four of the three classic zones become scar, and the RV’s fast inner layer conducts at 1.0 instead of 1.46 m/s, so in the computed activation the wave reaches the surviving muscle late and by winding paths. The last islands of surviving muscle activate about 105 ms after the QRS begins, but they are too small to produce a visible deflection. On the tracing the QRS still ends about 80 ms after its onset, and terminal activation in V1 and V2 is under 40 ms, close to the normal heart’s, so the 55 ms criterion is not met. In this chapter the QRS and terminal activation are read off the drawn leads, as a reader measures them; other chapters time the QRS from the simulated activation times, which in a heart without scar gives a few milliseconds more. No separate epsilon wave emerges either. The T-wave inversion is a modelling choice: the outer layer of the RV wall recovers after the inner layer, the reverse of normal.

Cardiac amyloidosis

Amyloid deposits thicken the walls without adding working muscle. An ESC position statement lists QRS voltage that is low for the degree of wall thickness as a red flag. In an early series, S in V1 plus R in V5 or V6 was 14.6 mm (normal 15 to 35 mm) while LV muscle area was increased, 11.4 cm²/m² (normal 6 to 10); voltage and muscle area were inversely related (r = −0.79). In 127 patients with light-chain (AL) amyloidosis and biopsy-proven cardiac involvement, 46% had low voltage, 47% a pseudoinfarct pattern and 16% met criteria for hypertrophy. Low voltage was defined in one study of 200 patients as a QRS of 0.5 mV or less in every limb lead, 1.0 mV or less in every chest lead, or a Sokolow-Lyon index of 1.5 mV or less; it was found in 34%, 13% and 60% by those three definitions and was a relatively late finding. The simulated LV walls are 15 mm thick (the RV wall keeps its 4 mm), and each ventricular cell makes 40% of the normal action-potential amplitude, a chosen value that stands in for fewer working cells in the same volume.

Pericardial effusion

Tamponade gives “decreased electrocardiographic voltage with electrical alternans”, attributed to the damping effect of the pericardial fluid and the swinging heart. The simulation represents both directly but approximately: one damping factor (0.45) scales every lead, and the heart’s orientation swings by 12° and 8° each way on alternate beats. Both values are chosen to make the signs visible; the true effect depends on the volume of fluid and the torso, and a real heart also moves toward and away from the chest wall.

Acute pulmonary embolism

In a meta-analysis of 45 studies and 8,209 patients, a heart rate over 100 was found in 38%, T-wave inversion in V1 in 38%, ST elevation in aVR in 36%, T-wave inversion in V1 to V4 in 29%, S1Q3T3 (an S wave in lead I, a Q wave and an inverted T wave in lead III) in 24%, atrial fibrillation in 15%, incomplete RBBB in 12% and complete RBBB in 10%. In 10 of these studies (3,007 patients), a fast rate, S1Q3T3, complete RBBB, inversion in V1 to V4, ST elevation in aVR and atrial fibrillation were associated with shock or death, though weakly for two of them: for inversion in V1 to V4 the pooled odds ratio was 1.69, with a 95% confidence interval of 0.83 to 3.43 that includes no effect, and complete RBBB lost significance when one study was left out. In an earlier series of patients with embolism and no prior heart or lung disease, the commonest ECG abnormality was nonspecific ST-segment or T-wave change, in 49%. Signs of RV overload are usually found in more severe cases; in milder embolism the only abnormality may be sinus tachycardia. The simulated heart beats at 110 per minute, with a dilated RV and a right bundle that conducts 30 ms late, and the QRS changes are computed from these. The T-wave inversion is again a modelling choice: the outer layer of the RV wall recovers after the inner layer. The normal simulated heart already has a small S wave in I and a small q wave in III; the simulated embolism deepens the S and inverts the T in III.
keypoints: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy: walls of 15 mm or more; T-wave inversion is far commoner than voltage criteria alone.

Arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy: in the 2010 task force criteria, T-wave inversion in V1–V3 and epsilon waves are major criteria and a terminal activation of 55 ms or more is minor; the 2023 ESC guideline advises caution with epsilon waves.
Amyloidosis: QRS voltage low for the wall thickness; frank low voltage in only about half of patients, and late.
Tamponade: low voltage with electrical alternans, from the damping fluid and the swinging heart.

Pulmonary embolism: of the right-heart signs pooled in one meta-analysis, a rate over 100 and T-wave inversion in V1 were the most frequent (38% each), and in milder embolism sinus tachycardia may be the only one; nonspecific ST–T change, not among them, was the most common abnormality in an earlier series (49%). T-wave inversion in V1–V4, S1Q3T3 and right bundle branch block are usually found in more severe cases.

chapters.title: Pacing
chapters.subtitle: Lead position, modes and malfunction
chapters.lede: A paced beat starts where the lead touches the heart: from right ventricular muscle it spreads slowly and the QRS is wide, from the His or left bundle it uses the conduction system. On a rhythm strip, the spikes show when the device paced and whether it captured and sensed correctly.
chapters.body:
The pacing code

Pacing modes are named by the generic code of the North American Society of Pacing and Electrophysiology and the British Pacing and Electrophysiology Group (the NBG code). The first letter is the chamber paced and the second the chamber sensed, each O (none), A (atrium), V (ventricle) or D (dual); the third is the response to a sensed event, O (none), T (triggered), I (inhibited) or D (dual); the fourth is R for rate modulation; the fifth marks multisite pacing in the atrium, the ventricle or both. The 2002 revision limited the fourth position to the presence or absence of rate modulation and the fifth to the location or absence of multisite pacing. The decoder above the cards takes any code; click a letter to change it.

Where the lead sits

A stimulus in the right ventricular (RV) muscle starts the wave where the lead tip touches, and the wave crosses the ventricles through muscle. From the RV apex the QRS is broad: in one series of 252 patients the paced QRS from the apical septum averaged 148.9 ms, and the series’ example apical tracing has a superior axis. From the RV septum the paced QRS has notches in the lateral leads, a “W” in V1 and a V6 R-wave peak time over 120 ms.

His bundle pacing uses the conduction system, and a 2018 working group standardized the definitions of its forms. The lead sits where the interval from the His potential to the QRS is 35 ms or more. When only the His bundle is captured (selective capture) an isoelectric interval follows the spike in all 12 leads, as long as the His-ventricular (HV) interval, and the QRS is identical to the native one; when the muscle beside it is captured too (non-selective capture), the QRS starts at the spike with a pseudo-delta wave. The simulation shows selective capture.

Left bundle branch area pacing (LBBAP) captures the left side of the septum, with or without the conduction system, from a lead screwed deep into the septum about 1 to 2 cm from the His bundle. The left ventricle is activated through the left bundle, while the right ventricle activates only after the wave crosses the septum: V1 ends with an R wave (qR, Qr, QR or rSR′), a sign that is sensitive for LBBAP but not specific for left bundle capture. Capture is judged by the time from the stimulus to the peak of the R wave in V6: under 75 ms with a narrow native QRS or isolated right bundle branch block, under 80 ms with left bundle branch block or a wide escape rhythm. Both cut-offs were 100% specific in their groups; the first was only about 40% sensitive. In the simulation the captured left bundle activates the left ventricle’s conduction system 30 ms after the stimulus, the middle of the 25 to 34 ms interval from left bundle potential to QRS reported for left bundle pacing; switch capture off to pace the septal muscle alone.

For cardiac resynchronization a second lead paces the left ventricle (LV) from a lateral coronary vein, on the epicardium. Biventricular pacing from the RV apex and a lateral vein gave a dominant R wave in V1 in 65% of 181 patients with left bundle branch block, and a Q or q wave in lead I in 85%; their absence did not necessarily mean a problem. At implant, a lead I complex that is neither QS nor QR is one of the findings listed for changing approach.

In this simulation a wave that enters the conduction system from the muscle travels through it slowly, so paced complexes are wide; the RV apical QRS is 165 ms. The widths also come in the wrong order: Gupta 2018 found the paced QRS narrower from the mid-septum and the outflow tract septum than from the apical septum, but the simulated RV septal QRS, 177 ms, is wider than the apical one. Burri 2023 describes the paced QRS narrowing as the lead advances from the right side of the septum to the left, but in the simulation pacing the left septal muscle alone gives 188 ms, wider still, and capturing the left bundle gives 172 ms, only 5 ms narrower than RV septal pacing, because the right ventricle, reached through the septum, finishes late. The simulated RV septal stimulus to V6 R-peak time is 110 ms, short of the more than 120 ms that Burri 2023 describes. The spikes are drawn at one fixed size.

Modes on a rhythm strip

AAI paces and senses the atrium and is inhibited by a sensed P wave; the ventricles then activate through the patient’s own atrioventricular (AV) node and conduction system. AAI cannot pace patients who develop atrial arrhythmias, and such an arrhythmia can leave them without backup pacing. VVI paces the ventricle when no QRS is sensed at the set rate; DDD senses both chambers and paces either or both. In the strips the lower rate is set to 60 per minute, the ventricular lead sits at the RV apex and the atrial lead in the right atrial appendage. Beneath the strip is the device’s marker channel, its record of what it sensed and paced: AS and AP for a sensed or paced atrial event, VS and VP for the ventricle, and, in rose on a third line, anything a channel sensed that was not its own chamber’s activity. On a narrow screen the strip shows the 6 seconds around the events its note describes.

When pacing fails

In failure to capture the device fires and the spikes appear, but the chamber does not depolarize, so the heart rate stays below the set rate. An undersensing device fails to detect the underlying rhythm, so it paces without regard to where the heart is in its cycle; a ventricular spike can fall on the T wave, the R-on-T phenomenon, which can lead to ventricular fibrillation. An oversensing device counts low-voltage deflections as P waves or QRS complexes and withholds pacing it should deliver; in a patient who depends on the pacemaker, oversensing of electromagnetic interference can cause asystole. In the simulation the oversensed signals are the heart’s own: P waves on the ventricular channel, or the QRS on the atrial channel. A spike that falls before the end of the previous T wave does not capture, because the simulated muscle is still refractory.
keypoints: The NBG code gives the chamber paced, the chamber sensed and the response (O, T, I, D), then rate modulation (R) and multisite pacing.
From an RV lead the wave spreads through muscle: a wide QRS and, from the septum, notched lateral leads and a “W” in V1.
Selective His capture gives an isoelectric interval after the spike and a QRS identical to the native one.
With left bundle area pacing V1 ends in an R wave; a stimulus to V6 R-peak time under 75 ms (narrow native QRS) or 80 ms (left bundle branch block) is specific for left bundle capture.
Failure to capture: spikes without a complex. Undersensing: spikes in the wrong place, including on the T wave. Oversensing: pacing withheld, and pauses.

chapters.title: AI-ECG
chapters.subtitle: A real network reads a simulated heart
chapters.lede: The network on this page learned from about 17,000 real electrocardiograms (ECGs) and runs in your browser. Choose a simulated heart to see the network’s five outputs and where in the tracing its answer is most sensitive.
chapters.body:
The model on this page

PTB-XL (version 1.0.3) is a public collection of 21,799 ten-second, 12-lead ECGs from 18,869 patients; its first release, described in 2020, held 21,837 from 18,885. Each record was labelled by up to two cardiologists or, for about a quarter, possibly only by the ECG machine’s automatic interpretation, with statements that group into five diagnostic superclasses: normal (NORM), myocardial infarction (MI), ST/T change (STTC), conduction disturbance (CD) and hypertrophy (HYP). Its records come split into ten folds by patient; the last two hold only records a person reviewed, and the standard practice is to train on folds 1 to 8, tune on fold 9 and test once on fold 10. The network here is a small one-dimensional convolutional network of about 275,000 parameters, written for this site and trained that way on the 100-samples-per-second recordings. On the 2,158 test records its macro area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC), the average over the five superclasses, is 0.93, in line with the published benchmark for this task. It reads 2.5-second windows, half-overlapping, and keeps each output's highest score across the ten seconds.

Reading a simulated heart

The network has never seen a simulated tracing. Each heart in the menu is a variant of the same simulated heart, so the network’s output is a test of transfer from real patients to a model of physiology. It reads the normal heart as normal; left bundle branch block (LBBB), right bundle branch block (RBBB) and left anterior fascicular block (LAFB) as conduction disturbances; and the scar and the acute inferior injury as infarction. It reads a left ventricle (LV) with 15 mm walls as normal and flags hypertrophy only at 19 mm, much as the voltage criteria for hypertrophy miss most thickened ventricles in patients. For the fascicular block its infarction output is nearly as high as its conduction output, and it reads the pre-excited heart as infarction. It misses the acute anterior injury and reads it as normal. In this simulation that injury raises the ST segment without Q waves in V1 to V4, while the inferior injury it catches also has Q waves about 40 ms wide in III and aVF. PTB-XL does hold acute infarcts, but where it gives an infarct’s stage, most are subacute or old. It reads the hyperkalemic heart as normal too. PTB-XL has no potassium label: electrolyte effects appear only in 96 records marked “electrolytic disturbance or drug”, filed under ST/T change, and that output stays near zero here.

What ECG networks can detect

Networks trained on thousands to millions of ECGs, an approach called artificial intelligence ECG (AI-ECG), detect conditions and traits that are hard to judge by eye. In Attia's Mayo Clinic work, an ECG network detected a left ventricular ejection fraction of 35% or less with an AUROC of 0.93; in a pragmatic trial in primary care, giving clinicians that result raised new diagnoses of an ejection fraction of 50% or less within 90 days from 1.6% to 2.1%. Networks have found atrial fibrillation from an ECG in sinus rhythm (AUROC 0.87), sex (AUROC 0.97) and age, hyperkalemia from two limb leads (AUROC 0.85 to 0.88 at three sites), hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (0.96), cardiac amyloidosis (0.91) and structural heart disease as defined by echocardiography (0.85 at the training hospitals), where the network also outperformed cardiologists in a controlled evaluation.

Where the output is sensitive

The lower panel, a saliency map, colours each lead by the gradient of the chosen output with respect to each sample of the input: how much the output would change if that point of the tracing moved. Among the explanation methods compared for ECG networks, this plain gradient was the one that pointed to specific moments in the tracing. It shows where an output is sensitive and does not say why; explanations of this kind have been called a false hope for judging an individual patient’s prediction, and they do not replace validation.

Domain shift

Performance measured where a model was trained often falls when it moves to another hospital, device or population (a domain shift), so it must be measured again there. Structural heart disease detection fell from 0.85 to between 0.78 and 0.80 at external sites; a kidney disease model fell from 0.77 to 0.71; in the 2020 PhysioNet challenge, top algorithms scored lower on the hidden test data, and lowest, on average, on the one institution held back entirely; and a heart failure model performed worse in some groups, notably young Black women. Reading simulated ECGs is a domain shift too, and it may account for some of the network’s misreadings of the simulated hearts.
keypoints: The network on this page is a real model, trained on PTB-XL’s recommended folds; it scores a macro AUROC of 0.93 on the held-out test fold.
It reads most simulated hearts as their diagnosis, but misses ST elevation without Q waves and reads the hyperkalemic heart as normal.
AI-ECG can detect low ejection fraction, atrial fibrillation from an ECG in sinus rhythm, amyloidosis and structural heart disease, findings that are hard to judge by eye.
A saliency map shows where an output is sensitive and does not say why.
Performance can drop at new hospitals and in some patient groups: validate a model where it will be used.
